title: How China can muddle through to superpower status
description: Despite structural challenges, China could rely on its economic and technological engine to become a peerless superpower in 2036, experts believe.
fullText:
Analysis of China is often so polarized that a casual observer might get the impression that Beijing is an unstoppable force on the verge of global domination a precarious dictatorship on the brink of collapse. That is not an impossible combination, of course. The Soviet Union was an archetypal fragile superpower, its red star burning bright before its dramatic final implosion. But China is a very different case, given its economic resilience, its technological advancement, its lack of interest in exporting ideology, and its reluctance to become entangled in foreign adventures.

So what does China's trajectory as a global power look like over the next decade? What kind of power will China be? And how fragile is it?

As a think-tank research director, I've sat in countless workshops and briefings with politicians, officials, investors, and wonks grappling with questions such as these. Most of the time, people come with their pre-existing views and biases, repeat them out loud, close their minds to alternative perspectives, and go home even more sure of their ways.

To move beyond these limitations, at Chatham House, we've been trying to corral bright minds on China and Asia's other rising powers to engage with a new way of thinking about the future: back-casting. It's the inverse of forecasting, where you start in the present and look forwards. With back-casting, you begin with a hypothetical future scenario — often a highly desirable or highly undesirable one — and then work backwards to ask, "How did we get here?"

Attempting to shed light on what kind of global power China might become, we brought together around 20 experts from government, business, and academia and presented them with a picture of China as a peerless technological-economic superpower in 2036.

In this scenario, which most participants thought highly plausible, Beijing has taken advantage of a faltering US and a divided Europe to parlay its dominance in manufacturing, robotics, and AI into unrivalled geopolitical power. It has recycled vast profits to buttress its global leadership ambitions, rebalancing international rules and institutions in its favor.

When we discussed the hurdles to China's progress, policymakers reeled off a long list of challenges: an aging population, local government debts, the ailing property market, youth unemployment, over-centralization of power by Xi Jinping, and the failure to establish a clear succession plan for the Communist Party.

This is standard fare for China watchers. What was unusual was when we pressed participants about whether these problems were really so serious and intractable that they could halt China's rise over the next 10 years: Apart from a few dissenters, most of our participants thought that China could, in fact, rely on its economic and technological engine to ride out these storms.

Advanced robotics and a rapid rollout of AI should counter the shrinking workforce, while creating enough new jobs to keep youth disaffection at bay. China's dominance of global manufacturing should keep the foreign exchange flowing in, allowing Beijing to manage bad debts in the property and local government sectors. And, despite some disquiet at Xi's massing of power and reluctance to lay out a succession plan, the Party seems sufficiently institutionalized and united around key objectives to navigate some future turbulence in leadership transition.

In sum, China's immense scale, national unity, deep political control, and increasingly cutting-edge technology may well allow it to sustain superpower status, even if it fails to resolve long-standing structural difficulties.

In some ways, this should not be so surprising: Although geopolitical analysts love to talk about turning points, crossroads, and dilemmas, many governments have a prosaic tendency to defy these dramatic predictions and muddle through.

So what can be done? Our scenario was predicated on the US continuing to turn inwards and failing to cooperate effectively with its network of allies in Europe and Asia. We also assumed that Europe would not get its collective act together.

Policymakers and voters in the US, Europe, and Asia have the power, collectively, to change this. In Washington, it is a truism that the only thing Congress can agree on is strong pushback against China. But, notwithstanding President Donald Trump's many about-turns on China policy, in the medium and long term, the US cannot shape China's prospects without the help of its allies.

The tightening of the vise around Taiwan, China's chokehold on rare earths, and Beijing's leaps forward on AI, semiconductors, and robotics have not been the wake-up calls they should have been. What the US and its allies need is another "Sputnik moment," where Beijing shocks them into action by some spectacular feat of innovation, perhaps developing a cure for an intractable disease, developing globally dominant AI applications, or unveiling solar-powered data centers in space.

Ironically, it may take more successes from Beijing to snap Europe and the US out of their complacency, in the case of the former, and self-centricity and self-harm in the case of the latter.

Yuan revaluation, enforced through tariffs, may be the only way to prevent China's "monstrous and growing trade surplus" from swamping the West's native industries, Greg Ip argued in The Wall Street Journal.

title: Driscoll breaks silence after resigning as Army secretary
description: Dan Driscoll broke his silence late Tuesday, announcing that his last full day as Army secretary will be Wednesday, but he did not offer a reason for why he is resigning from the post he has held for ...
fullText:
Dan Driscoll broke his silence late Tuesday, announcing that his last full day as Army secretary will be Wednesday, but he did not offer a reason for why he is resigning from the post he has held for 18 months.

"As a third-generation Army veteran, it has been the honor of a lifetime to serve as the Secretary of the Army under President Trump and Secretary Hegseth. Tomorrow is my last full day in the role," Driscoll said in a post on the social platform X. "Our Soldiers, Civilians and their Families are our Nation's very best, and they have inspired me every day. I am sincerely thankful for their service and sacrifice."

"I had the privilege of working with them to modernize and accelerate how the Army mans, trains, and equips the most lethal fighting force on the face of the earth. We could not have made the progress we did without the support of Secretary Hegseth," Driscoll continued, praising the Pentagon chief, with whom he has had tensions since the two got to the Pentagon in early 2025.

"I am forever grateful to President Trump for the opportunity to once again serve my country," he added.

Driscoll went to the White House on Monday and spoke with the president about the "current state" of the Army before tendering his resignation, The Hill and other news outlets reported.

Driscoll's departure underlines how Hegseth is imposing his will and consolidating power at the Pentagon.

Apart from the turf war Driscoll has been embroiled in with Hegseth, the Defense secretary has ousted several senior Army leaders with whom the Army secretary has worked o modernize the service branch's warfighting efforts.

The Army's vice chief of staff, Gen. James Mingus, retired without explanation in October. Hegseth then fired the Army's chief of staff, Gen. Randy George, and in June Gen. Chris Donahue, the commander of U.S. Army Europe and Africa, retired.

Gen. Christopher LaNeve, who was Hegseth's military adviser, has been serving as the Army's acting chief of staff since George's removal.

The Pentagon is looking to confirm LaNeve, the former commander of the 82nd Airborne Division at Fort Bragg, N.C., as Army chief of staff, but the potential nomination is facing objections from senators in both parties.

Driscoll cultivated relationships with lawmakers in both parties on Capitol Hill. Some of those same lawmakers were unhappy with his departure from the administration, criticizing Hegseth for firing or sidelining more than two dozen senior military officers since taking the helm at the Pentagon.

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he was "disappointed" to learn of Driscoll's departure.

"I'm hearing the same rumors everybody else is: that he was frustrated with some of his top generals being released," Rounds told reporters on Tuesday, adding, "that's not the first time I've heard that."

title: Kremlin says Putin, Xi and Trump may hold a trilateral meeting in November
description: MOSCOW, Sept 1 (Reuters) - Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said on Tuesday that Russian President Vladimir Putin, U.S.
fullText:
MOSCOW, Sept 1 (Reuters) - Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said on Tuesday that Russian ‌President Vladimir Putin, U.S. President Donald ‌Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping may hold ​a trilateral meeting at the next Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November.

Asked on state TV about the possibility of such a meeting, ‌Ushakov said: "This ⁠issue was discussed, yes."

He said all three leaders were expected to ⁠attend the summit, adding: "And if it turns out as has been said, then the ​three of ​them will be ​able to have a ‌meeting."

Ushakov was speaking from the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek, where Putin and Xi had attended a gathering of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation.

Russia, China and the United States are part ‌of the 21-member APEC. ​Shenzhen, China, will host ​the next ​leaders' summit November 18-19.

"We have no ‌announcements regarding President Trump's ​attendance at ​APEC at this time," White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said.

title: Lula's lead over Flavio Bolsonaro narrows ahead of Brazil election, Quaest poll shows
description: SAO PAULO, Sept 2 (Reuters) - Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's lead over right-wing challenger Senator Flavio Bolsonaro narrowed further ahead of October's election, a Quaest poll
fullText:
SAO PAULO, Sept 2 (Reuters) - Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's lead over right-wing challenger Senator ‌Flavio Bolsonaro narrowed further ahead of October's election, a ‌Quaest poll commissioned by Globo showed on Wednesday.

• In a simulated second-round ​runoff, Lula would win 42% of the vote, compared with 41% for the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.

• Quaest called this a technical tie, as its poll has a ‌margin of error of ⁠2 percentage points.

• An earlier Quaest poll released on August 14 had Lula leading Bolsonaro by 43% ⁠to 40%.

• In a first-round scenario, Lula would lead with 37% of the votes, followed by Bolsonaro (30%), Augusto Cury (10%) and Renan ​Santos (3%).

• Quaest ​is the third major survey ​this week to show ‌author and psychiatrist Cury in third place, as TV appearances and strong social media reach have lifted his standing in polls.

• If no candidate wins more than 50% of valid votes in the first round, the two frontrunners advance to a ‌runoff.

• Quaest surveyed 2,004 people ​between August 30 and September 1.

• ​This is the first ​Quaest poll released since the start of the ‌television and radio political campaign.

• It ​also comes after ​new developments in an investigation involving Lula's son, Fabio Luis Lula da Silva, over allegations he improperly assisted ​a lobbyist in ‌dealings with the Health Ministry. Lula's son has denied ​the allegations.

title: All 16 of Russia's latest satellites for its Starlink rival failed to reach their intended orbit
description: The 16 satellites form the second batch of the Rassvet-3 constellation, which now only has 12 out of 32 launched satellites set for long-term orbit.
fullText:
After being cut off from Starlink, Russia is pushing to build its own version of the service.

But publicly available data shows its latest batch of 16 satellites hasn't reached operational orbit.

That's out of a total of 32 satellites launched so far, for a 37.5% success rate for now.

An entire batch of Russian low Earth orbit satellites, intended to help create Moscow's version of Starlink, has failed to reach or remain at their anticipated altitudes just over a month after launch.

The 16 Rassvet-3 satellites, launched on July 19, were originally supposed to orbit the Earth at an altitude of roughly 500 miles, according to the company developing the constellation, Bureau 1440.

But publicly available US Space Force data shows that, as of Tuesday, the Rassvet-3 satellites are instead orbiting at altitudes of between 190 miles and 250 miles.

Atmospheric drag at that altitude significantly shortens a satellite's operational lifespan. Without intervention, those conditions gradually pull satellites lower to Earth until they reenter the atmosphere and burn up or break apart.

Losing these 16 satellites — Bureau 1440's second batch of the Rassvet-3 — would be a significant setback for Moscow's ambition to create its own alternative to Starlink, a priority for the Kremlin after SpaceX cut off satellite internet service to Russian forces on February 1.

Rassvet-3 is meant to help fill that gap, but Bureau 1440 has launched only 32 satellites so far, including this latest batch.

Issues with the second satellite batch were first highlighted by journalist Anatoly Zak, who runs the website RussianSpaceWeb and identified two Rassvet-3 satellites in early August that were already headed for re-entry into Earth's atmosphere.

It's unclear what prevented the satellites from reaching higher altitudes. Positional data indicates that many of them engaged in maneuvers to climb upward, though none of these appear to have come close to helping the satellites reach their operational orbit yet.

"The apparent failure of all 16 satellites from the second launch to reach their intended operational altitudes suggests Russia may have been unprepared to accelerate constellation deployment at this pace and will likely face additional delays," wrote analysts from the Institute for the Study of War, a US-based think tank, on Monday.

Press services for Bureau 1440 and Roscosmos, Russia's space agency, did not immediately respond to comment requests sent outside regular business hours by Business Insider.

Bureau 1440 has said that it is planning "dozens of launches and hundreds of satellites" to form its total constellation.

Its first batch of 16, launched on March 23, saw 12 satellites reach and maintain altitudes of about 340 miles. That's still shy of the original 500-mile altitude that Russia initially set, and could indicate that Bureau 1440 shifted the target orbit closer to Earth.

Ukrainian estimates say the Kremlin will need roughly 200 to 250 operational satellites to maintain a stable internet network that Russian forces can use to communicate or operate combat drones.

SpaceX, by comparison, runs over 11,000 operational Starlink satellites.

A major bottleneck for the Rassvet-3 constellation is how they're launched. Russian spacecraft rely on the Soyuz-2.1b rocket, which has been used for 104 launches in the last two decades.

With 16 satellites per launch, keeping to that pace would mean Russia could launch roughly 80 Rassvet-3 satellites each year, taking more than two years to reach a constellation of at least 200.

And that assumes all the launched satellites remain operational in the long term.

With only 12 of the last 32 Rassvet-3 satellites reaching their apparent long-term orbits, the program has achieved a 37.5% success rate so far. SpaceX, by comparison, reported just 43 early mission failures or terminations among its first 1,383 production Starlink satellites, or a failure rate of about 3%.

Ukraine has also been attempting to undermine Russia's efforts. In mid-August, it said one of its FP-5 Flamingo long-range missiles struck a space center in Western Russia that produces the Soyuz rocket.

Satellite internet has become one of the most crucial communications tools of the war in Ukraine, with troops from both sides using the service to stay in contact with each other, direct drones, and update commanders.

Most prominently, Russia was previously found to be using Starlink terminals to relay signals to its attack drones, allowing them to bypass typical jamming measures and receive instructions at extended range.

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

title: Lindsay Clancy jury says it's still deadlocked, judge gives 'dynamite instruction'
description: Judge William Sullivan urged jurors in the triple murder trial of Lindsay Clancy to keep deliberating after they twice reported being deadlocked.
fullText:
This article discusses suicide and suicidal ideation. If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. Call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org.

Jurors in the triple murder trial of Massachusetts mother Lindsay Clancy must continue deliberations after the judge made a last ditch attempt to break their deadlock on Sept. 2.

If the jury can't reach a unanimous verdict, Judge William Sullivan will declare a mistrial, leaving prosecutors to decide whether to retry Clancy. Jurors have been asked to rethink their positions on the case under court instructions.

Clancy, 36, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of murder in the January 2023 strangulation deaths of her three children – Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months – at the family's Duxbury, Massachusetts, home. The jury began deliberating on Aug. 27 after hearing weeks of testimony from more than 80 witnesses.

Around 10 a.m. ET on Sept. 1, the group of nine women and three men notified Sullivan they have not been able to reach a unanimous decision. Sullivan urged them to continue deliberating, and they did so until 3:30 p.m. ET when they asked to leave early for the day.

But after deliberating until nearly 2:30 p.m. ET on Sept. 2, the jury informed Sullivan that they were still at an impasse. Sullivan gave them what's known as a Tuey-Rodriguez charge, a special set of instructions similar to an Allen charge. The instructions, which were refined in and named for two Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court cases, ask jurors on each side to rethink their position and "consider that it is desirable that the case be decided."

"You have been selected in the same manner, and from the same source, as any future jury would be," Sullivan said. "There is no reason to suppose that the case will ever be submitted to twelve persons who are more intelligent, more impartial, or more competent to decide it or that more or clearer evidence will be produced."

Daniel Medwed, a professor of law and criminal justice at Northeastern University, told USA TODAY the message is sometimes called a "dynamite instruction" because the forceful language is intended to break the deadlock.

"It really is designed to encourage the jury to take one last look at things and really try," Medwed said.

Prosecutors allege Clancy planned the killings by sending her husband out on errands and then strangling the children with exercise bands while he was gone. Clancy then cut her wrists and neck and jumped out of a second-story window, leaving her paralyzed.

Clancy's attorney, Kevin Reddington, has not denied that she killed her children but has argued she is not guilty of murder because she lacks criminal responsibility – more commonly known as an insanity defense. Reddington said she was struggling with postpartum depression and psychosis at the time of the killings.

If the jury cannot come to a unanimous consensus about Clancy's guilt after more deliberations, the judge will declare a mistrial. Prosecutors will then have to decide whether to retry Clancy in front of a new jury.

Reddington told reporters outside the courthouse he expected prosecutors to bring charges against Clancy again in the event of a mistrial.

"Tim Cruz will never drop it, that's for sure," Reddington said, referring to Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz.

That's what happened when another recent high-profile murder case in Massachusetts ended with a hung jury.

Jurors deliberating the fate of Karen Read following the death of her boyfriend, Boston police officer John O'Keefe, twice told Judge Beverly Cannone they were unable to reach a verdict. After getting the Tuey-Rodriguez instruction, the jury remained deadlocked and Cannone declared a mistrial in July 2024.

Prosecutors decided to retry Read, and she was acquitted of the most serious charges, second-degree murder and leaving the scene of a collision resulting in death, by a new jury in June 2025.

The beginning of deliberations on Sept. 2 was delayed slightly as the judge appeared to address the arrest of a woman who allegedly took video of jurors outside the courthouse.

Dawn Light, 56, was arrested around 3:40 p.m. on Sept. 1 and charged with one count of intimidation of a witness, jurors, or person furnishing information in connection with criminal proceedings, according to state police.

During Light's arraignment on Sept. 2, a prosecutor said state police who were providing security during the Clancy trial were notified about a person in a restricted area outside the courthouse and encountered Light in her vehicle in a parking lot. Light denied taking any photos in the area, but when officers looked through her phone, they found video of jurors exiting the building that had been recently deleted.

An attorney representing Light said the incident was a misunderstanding and that the retired registered nurse was trying to get a picture of Clancy, not the jury. A not guilty plea was entered on Light's behalf, and she was ordered to return on Oct. 15 for a pretrial hearing.

Sullivan began proceedings in the Clancy trial on Sept. 2 by reminding spectators that there are court orders in place, as well as state statutes that relate to jurors, witnesses and attorneys.

"Everyone should be well aware that that order and that statute is being enforced and will be enforced," Sullivan said. "I just want to put that out there without editorial comment."

Sullivan then spoke to jurors individually at sidebar in the presence of the attorneys before allowing them to resume deliberations around 9:30 a.m. ET.

There are several options on the verdict slip in the Clancy trial:

Not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility

Guilty of murder in the first degree

Guilty of murder in the second degree

If the jury finds Lindsay Clancy guilty, it must also determine what degree of murder she should be convicted of.

The degree of the murder conviction would impact the length of a prison sentence; if she is convicted of first-degree murder, it carries a mandatory life sentence in Massachusetts.

If the jury finds her not guilty or lacking criminal responsibility, under Massachusetts law, the sentence typically requires the defendant to undergo a mental evaluation and likely a commitment to a state hospital for treatment.

Clancy has been held at Tewksbury Hospital, a facility in Tewksbury, Massachusetts, for court-ordered mental health treatment since May 2023.

Contributing: Jessica Trufant and Brad Petrishen, The Patriot Ledger

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Lindsay Clancy jury says it's still deadlocked, judge gives 'dynamite instruction'

title: Kennedy Center removes 'Blue' sculpture as Trump presses on with Washington makeover
description: WASHINGTON, Sept 2 (Reuters) - A crane removed the 24-foot (7-meter) sculpture "Blue" from the Kennedy Center grounds on Wednesday in the latest move to redesign Washington's public spaces under
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Sept 2 (Reuters) - A crane removed the 24-foot (7-meter) sculpture "Blue" from the Kennedy Center grounds on Wednesday in the latest move to redesign ‌Washington's public spaces under President Donald Trump.

The sculpture, made of rectangular blue aluminum ‌blocks, had sat near where a tarp obscures the center's facade, as Trump allies continue court battles ​to try to keep his name on the front of the complex, created by an act of Congress to memorialize slain President John F. Kennedy.

Created by artist Joel Shapiro, "Blue" resembles a soaring stick figure with arms outstretched and one leg kicked up ‌in the air. Since 2019, ⁠it was located on a grassy area between the main Kennedy Center building and a separate venue called "The Reach" used for ⁠arts education.

The Kennedy Center confirmed in a statement that the statue would be removed and said artwork deinstallations were common practice.

"We are deeply grateful to Joel Shapiro for ​the years ​Blue has spent animating our campus and ​connecting visitors to his vision," a ‌Kennedy Center spokesperson said.

Trump is pursuing an ambitious remaking of Washington, with plans for projects ranging from a new White House ballroom, which he calls a national security priority, to a 250-foot (76-meter) arch. Administration lawyers argued in a court filing last week that the Kennedy Center could eventually face demolition without major repairs.

Since taking ‌office in 2025, Trump has removed the center's ​leadership, changed its programming and appointed a board ​that has closed the center ​for renovations. A U.S. district court judge ordered in May that ‌Trump's name be removed from the ​facade.

The Kennedy Center board, ​controlled by Trump appointees, subsequently voted on August 13 to put Trump's name back on the building, calling it "The John F. Kennedy Center for the ​Performing Arts Restored and ‌Renovated by President Donald J. Trump." This move has set up a ​potential clash with the judge.

title: Fox News host says Trump made her husband Transportation secretary ‘because that was all that’s left’
description: Fox News host Rachel Campos-Duffy on Tuesday said President Trump tapped her husband, Sean Duffy, to be Transportation secretary “because that was all that’s left.” The two were interviewed on “The Ka...
fullText:
Fox News host Rachel Campos-Duffy on Tuesday said President Trump tapped her husband, Sean Duffy, to be Transportation secretary "because that was all that's left."

The two were interviewed on "The Katie Miller Podcast," hosted by the wife of White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller. The host asked about their conversation after Trump nominated Duffy.

"He said he wanted to serve the president in any way," Campos-Duffy said. "He ended up in Transportation because that was all that's left."

Duffy, himself a former Fox News host, interjected and said he believed Trump when he told him, "If I wasn't the president, I would pick the Department of Transportation over any department. It's the best department, and I'm going to give it to you."

The secretary then emphasized Trump's focus on construction, having been a developer for much of his life, and said the U.S. has "a president who cares about the infrastructure of America. Usually, presidents don't give a darn."

Campos-Miller later said that given her closeness to the administration through her husband and role at Fox News, she does not "talk about anything to do with transportation, and Fox wouldn't want me to and I don't want to."

"It's no secret that Rachel Campos-Duffy loves President Donald Trump," she said, causing Miller to laugh. "I was with him when he came down the escalator [in New York City's Trump Tower in 2015]. I was very early on and even in the dark years when he was out of office and a lot of people had a lot of beef with him and he was facing all the criminal charges."

Duffy, who also served as NASA's acting administrator in 2025, and Campos-Duffy have been married since 1999.

The two host a reality series titled "The Great American Road Trip," which prompted the watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington to call on the Department of Transportation's Office of Inspector General to investigate Duffy's role in the show and whether he violated any federal regulations or laws in filming the series.

Campos-Duffy defended her husband, saying he's not a "corrupt man."

Duffy previously co-hosted Fox Business Network's "The Bottom Line" before Trump asked him to join his second administration. Campos-Duffy guest-hosted on Fox News's "Outnumbered" before she became a permanent co-host of "Fox & Friends Weekend" in 2021.

Trump also hired former "Fox & Friends Weekend" co-host Pete Hegseth to be Defense secretary and former Fox News host Dan Bongino to serve as deputy director of the FBI before he resigned in January.

Trump has long favored Fox News's coverage of his administrations, though not without some criticism when their coverage refers to his low approval rating or remarks from critics.

title: A Real-Life Romance (And The Love Of Fans) Fueled A Classic NES Remake
description: With headlines dominated by stories of buyouts, layoffs, employee mistreatment, and crunch, it's easy to think that game development is a constant parade of misery and strife. But the vast majority of developers still make games out of genuine love for the medium--and feel deeply connected to their teammates. The surprise announcement of a Steam remake of NES cult classic Battle of Olympus showcases the joyful side of game development: a project born of an idea that blossomed into a real-life romance, decade-long careers, and gratitude for the fans who have kept the game in peoples' minds.
fullText:
With headlines dominated by stories of buyouts, layoffs, employee mistreatment, and crunch, it’s easy to think that game development is a constant parade of misery and strife. But the vast majority of developers still make games out of genuine love for the medium–and feel deeply connected to their teammates. The surprise announcement of a Steam remake of NES cult classic Battle of Olympus showcases the joyful side of game development: a project born of an idea that blossomed into a real-life romance, decade-long careers, and gratitude for the fans who have kept the game in peoples’ minds.

The Battle of Olympus is a side-scrolling action-RPG released in 1988 by Broderbund for the NES. The visuals and gameplay take a lot of cues from Zelda II, though with a Greek mythology-inspired story and setting and a pretty solid challenge level throughout. It’s been described as “a hidden gem” of the NES library many times, often overshadowed by similar titles, but beloved by those who enjoyed it.

Notably, The Battle of Olympus was developed in Japan by a very small developer named Infinity. How small? Well, the game’s credits list a whopping three different people–Yukio Horimoto, Reiko Oshida, and Kazuo Sawa. Yukio and Reiko were the two main collaborators, with Yukio handling programming, Reiko on art design, and the pair working together on the game’s story. As it turns out, the project would lead the two to discover their connection to each other, and they would marry soon after–making it very fitting that The Battle of Olympus’s Japanese subtitle is “The Legend of Love.”

Infinity would grow and continue work as a contract developer, porting titles from series like Ultima and Doom to various platforms while also releasing original work like GameCube fan-favorite Ribbit King. However, it now appears that Yukio and Reiko are ready to retire, and they want to do so by re-releasing the game that both brought them together and put Infinity on the map. But, as the YouTube video announcement emphasizes, this wouldn’t have happened without the decades of support from fans of The Battle of Olympus, who continue to support the game through videos, streaming, and discussion.

It’s hard not to watch the announcement video with a smile on your face, with Reiko happily describing the game’s development, what it means to them, and how much fan support has touched them over such a long time. In a sea of depressing news, sometimes we need a love story to remind us why games can be so great.

title: Turkey's relations with Russia, China don't mean turning its back on the West, Erdogan says
description: Turkey is not backing away from the West as it seeks deeper ties with the East, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Wednesday as he headed back from a Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit....
fullText:
ISTANBUL (AP) — Turkey is not backing away from the West as it seeks deeper ties with the East, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Wednesday as he headed back from a Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit.

The conference in Kyrgyzstan saw Erdogan hold a one-on-one meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin at which they discussed further nuclear cooperation.

In comments made to journalists aboard the presidential plane, Erdogan reiterated Turkey's goal of becoming a full member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, or SCO, whose ten current members include Russia, China, India and Iran.

"I would also like to particularly emphasize that Turkey's membership perspective in the organization does not mean a break from a bloc or turning our backs on the West," the president said.

Turning to the war in Ukraine, during which Ankara has maintained friendly relations with both Moscow and Kyiv, Erdogan said it was his and Putin's "expectation … that the war between Russia and Ukraine ends peacefully as soon as possible."

He also underlined the importance of maritime security in the Black Sea, where civilian shipping has come under increasing attack.

"There is a need for a mechanism that will permanently ensure the safety of commercial maritime transport in the Black Sea," Erdogan said, adding that it would be "beneficial" to prevent a "resurgence of the grain crisis."

Turkey brokered a grain deal in 2022 that opened Ukrainian ports and allowed the movement of Russian food and fertilizer. The agreement, which Putin pulled out of a year later, was vital for global food supplies, especially in Africa, the Middle East and Asia.

The SCO, founded in 2001, also includes Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Pakistan and Belarus. The growing bloc has been billed as a counterweight to U.S. global influence, although its goals and programs remain vague.

title: Justice Department seizes more than $560,000 in cryptocurrency donations for Hamas
description: The FBI has seized more than $560,000 in cryptocurrency donations intended for Hamas, the Justice Department said Tuesday in announcing a disruption of financing for the militant group.  In addition t...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The FBI has seized more than $560,000 in cryptocurrency donations intended for Hamas, the Justice Department said Tuesday in announcing a disruption of financing for the militant group.

In addition to seizing cryptocurrency meant to support Hamas' military wing, the department said that it had taken control of website domains and communication platforms used for fundraising and recruitment, and had obtained information about thousands of people who had contacted Hamas with a goal of giving money to the group.

"My message to Hamas is clear: your networks are not secure, your crypto is vulnerable, and we will not stop until your ability to wage war is defeated," Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, said in a video statement announcing the operation.

According to FBI affidavits filed in connection with the seizures, Hamas began testing virtual currency fundraising in or around early 2019 through its Qassam Brigades, or military wing, and solicited donations on its Telegram channel and also used direct online fundraising. Hamas officials bragged that the currency would be untraceable and their websites offered instructions for how to make anonymous donations, the affidavits say.

A major investigative break arrived last year when FBI officials identified a financing network soliciting donations to the Qassam Brigades via virtual currency and a confidential source located in the United States alerted law enforcement to a Telegram post asking for contributions to an email address associated with Hamas.

Brett Leatherman, an FBI assistant director in charge of its cyber division, said the bureau would "continue to use its authorities to intercept illicit funds and prevent terrorist organizations from exploiting digital networks to finance their operations."

Hamas officials could not immediately be reached for comment.

title: Nation’s largest teachers union under fire as controversial agenda puts century-old federal charter at risk
description: Sen. Bill Cassidy's report targets the NEA's ties to the Zinn Education Project and Rethinking Schools over curriculum glorifying political violence.
fullText:
EXCLUSIVE — The head of an influential Senate committee is urging Congress to reconsider the charter of the nation's largest teachers union, citing its far-left associations and allegedly irresponsible financial activity.

In recent years, the National Education Association, which represents roughly 3 million educators, has come under fire for mobilizing students and teachers to support liberal activist campaigns, been criticized by its Jewish members for failing to address antisemitism, spent millions in membership dues supporting left-wing causes and partnered with organizations that portray political violence and far-left extremism favorably.

Now, Sen. Bill Cassidy, the Republican chair of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions, is calling on his colleagues to take a closer look at the NEA's congressional charter.

Blistering Report Exposes How National K-12 Group's Dei Agenda Is Trickling Down To Local Schools

"Children are struggling to read and to do basic math. Instead of helping students succeed, teachers' unions are injecting a dangerous, anti-American agenda into our classrooms," Cassidy told Fox News Digital. "Parents deserve to send their children to school without worrying that they will be indoctrinated with Dei and taught that Americans have 'misplaced faith' in our institutions."

Cassidy, in a report outlining the NEA's activity obtained exclusively by Fox News Digital, puts a spotlight on the Zinn Education Project and Rethinking Schools — a pair of interlinked educational nonprofits that the top teachers union has collaborated with extensively.

Exclusive: Splc's 'Far-left' 'Anti-racism' Curriculum Found In Classrooms As Early As Kindergarten: Watchdog

The Zinn Education Project and Rethinking Schools, for instance, have published curricular materials that justify the actions of the Black Panther Party — a left-wing militant Black nationalist organization that operated during the Cold War — and praise its members, including those who were involved in acts of political violence, according to the report.

"The Marxist and communist ideologies espoused by the Black Panther Party are inconsistent and incompatible with the foundation of the United States Constitution," Cassidy's report, published by the HELP committee, reads. "The Black Panthers advocated for the use of armed force against police and were involved in the murders of civil servants and members of their own party."

Scope Of Splc's Deeply Embedded Influence Training Teachers Nationwide Uncovered In Sweeping Report

Rethinking Schools also published a lesson plan where students are meant to role-play as "queer liberation" activists fighting against the "Religious Right," according to the report. Another lesson plan, titled "Expanding Intersectional Queer History in the Elementary Grades," instructs teachers on how to incorporate LGBTQ material into lessons for young students.

The union has worked closely with the duo of nonprofits over the years, giving them prominent space and speaking opportunities at conferences, collaborating with them on curriculum development and nationwide teaching events, and praising and promoting their lessons. The union has also incorporated the groups' work into educator handbooks and helped distribute their lesson plans to teachers.

House Gop Launches Probe Into 5 Major Labor Unions Over Dem Spending Despite Maga Membership Base

Congress chartered the NEA in 1906 under the expectation that it would "elevate the character and advance the interests of the profession of teaching; and to promote the cause of education in the United States," a mission Cassidy and some other Republicans argue it has since strayed from. Revoking the NEA's charter would primarily be a reputational blow to the union, as it would still be able to operate even without it.

As another example of the NEA allegedly failing to live up to its charter, the HELP committee points to its involvement in the left-wing protest movements.

May Day Protests 'Just The Beginning' Of Student Activism Push, Expert Warns

The labor union promoted and participated in the 2026 May Day protests, which were critical of President Donald Trump and his Republican allies. In one planning webinar the NEA hosted in the lead-up to the demonstrations, educators were advised to "bring activism into the classroom," targeting children as young as three years old. Students in Chicago were reportedly encouraged by teachers to skip class for the protests, even as Chicago Public Schools see subpar reading and math competency scores.

On the financial side of things, Cassidy points to data showing that, since 2015, the NEA has contributed hundreds of millions of dollars to advocacy organizations and political action committees, the vast majority of which are left-of-center. In some cases, political organizations funded by the NEA later provided members of the union's leadership team with cushy jobs, according to the report.

Far-left Activist Conference At Teachers Union Hq Raises Classroom Concerns

"The central issue is not whether every such expenditure is impermissible. Rather, it is whether members receive sufficient transparency about how their dues are used, whether union leadership has adopted adequate safeguards against conflicts of interest and whether these expenditures advance the purposes for which members joined the union in the first place," the Senate committee report reads.

Organizations funded by the NEA include the Sixteen Thirty Fund and the Tides Foundation, two of the largest Democratic-aligned dark money operations in the country, as well as millions to its own PAC, which almost exclusively supports Democratic candidates.

Jewish Educators Face Rampant Antisemitism In Teachers Unions, New Report Finds

The HELP committee report also alleges that the NEA has failed to represent the interests of Jewish educators, citing an August 2025 letter where the union's Jewish Affairs Caucus claimed its members reported "shunning, harassment and antisemitic comments" at the union's annual assembly.

While not congressionally chartered like the NEA, the American Federation of Teachers drew flak from Cassidy's report for many of the same reasons.

The report cites the AFT's participation in "No Kings" protests against President Donald Trump, its boycott of Target over immigration enforcement and its advocacy on LGBTQ+ issues, as well as its routing of tens of millions of dollars to liberal causes, as evidence of alleged mission drift at the union.

The NEA, AFT, Rethinking Schools and the Zinn Education Project did not respond to requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Tuesday.

The scrutiny comes as the NEA transitions to new leadership. Princess R. Moss, a former NEA vice president and secretary-treasurer, began a three-year term as president on Tuesday, succeeding Becky Pringle, who led the union for six years.

title: Old and On the Way: How Ed Markey Dispatched Seth Moulton in Massachusetts
description: Joan...
fullText:
Moulton, a centrist opportunist, sought to unseat his incumbent opponent by posturing as a young progressive. Voters didn’t fall for it.

Massachusetts Representative Seth Moulton was the last 2020 Democratic presidential candidate to speak at the Iowa State Fair “political soapbox” in August 2019, and I got to see him there. He delivered a lackluster speech before a relatively small audience. Hilariously, he told the crowd that “I had people talking to me at the urinal in the restroom, saying that they’re here to hear my speech.” My friends and I joked that we could feel the “Moultmentum.”

To no one’s surprise, Moulton left the primary race six days later—months before any votes were cast. In 2018, he had been a leader in a small centrist Democratic movement to block Nancy Pelosi from becoming speaker if Democrats took the House back in the midterms. After the party did, that Moulton campaign also went nowhere.

Moulton’s 2026 primary challenge to Democratic Senator Ed Markey met the same fate Tuesday night, when the progressive incumbent beat him by nearly a two-to-one margin. The Boston centrist, 47, tried to make the race a generational challenge against the 80-year-old Markey. But in fact, Moulton locked himself into the role of the old and out-of-touch guy, when two days after Kamala Harris lost to Donald Trump in 2024, he unburdened himself to The New York Times and announced that he disagreed with Harris and many Democrats’ progressive views, including staunch support for trans rights. “I have two little girls,” he said. “I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete. But as a Democrat, I’m supposed to be afraid to say that.” Markey quickly denounced him for throwing trans Americans “under the bus,” but Moulton insisted he was only speaking hard truths to a complacent progressive establishment. “I think that our refusal to engage in this debate, to answer the Republicans’ attacks, did a great disservice to the trans community,” he said.

These efforts to play to anti-trans sentiment within the Democratic party fell flat in Moulton’s Senate bid. At an October “No Kings” rally in Boston, Markey drew cheers, wearing a sheer trans scarf in pink and light blue, while Moulton was booed. As his trans-baiting ploys failed to gain any traction in his Senate bid, Moulton apologized to anyone who was hurt by his remarks and said he broadly supported trans rights. Still, he never took back his slam on trans athletes’ playing in women’s sports.

That wasn’t the only reason Markey won, but it was one of them. The larger reason Moulton lost is that he is a career centrist opportunist who kicked Harris while she was down, tried to take the gavel from Pelosi, and consistently blamed the party’s left for Trump’s two victories. Challenging Markey, he also tried to revive the broadly shared Democratic discomfort, especially in hindsight, with Biden running for reelection at 80, when he was clearly hobbled in speech and physical movement by his age (and diagnosed with late-stage prostate cancer once he left office.)

Sadly for Biden, there’s no comparison with Markey, who is well-spoken, witty, and agile. The incumbent senator also put together strong support from progressives, including fellow Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren, Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, Massachusetts Representative Ayanna Presley, and New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, all of whom joined him for a late rally on Sunday. Years ago, he backed Ocasio-Cortez when the Green New Deal was considered radical (it later drove some Biden policies), and he also backs Medicare for All, expanding Social Security, and higher taxes on the wealthy.

“This is the greatest gathering of progressive voices on one stage,” Markey told the crowd on Sunday. “Our progressive-palooza. That’s what we have put together.” But the real excitement came with Tuesday’s vote-a-palooza, when he won back his seat 65–35.

Moulton drew progressive ire for linking Markey to the late sex-abuser Jeffrey Epstein, charging him with “meeting with a lobbyist on behalf of…Epstein.” Markey angrily denied the charge, which was eventually disproven. Another supposed point Moulton scored in a debate with Markey—a gotcha exchange that had Markey confessing that he wasn’t sure he’d ever used artificial intelligence—also turned out to be a nonissue. “I use whatever is inside of my iPhone and my iPad, whatever comes up,” the senator said. “And I don’t know what company my iPad might be using.” It was an honest and fair answer: None of us truly know what kind of software our devices employ. But the absolutely correct answer would have been that the Big Tech companies are putting so much AI slop in their devices and apps, it leaves users adopting AI whether they want to or not.

Despite Moulton’s slaps at Pelosi and Harris, in this race he wanted to be known as a progressive. His campaign website features a “redbox”—a ploy that campaigns use to skirt campaign rules against coordinating with outside groups by placing approved messaging for other advertising initiatives or social-media promotions to adopt within a notionally unaffiliated red frame on their websites. Moulton’’s redbox said, “Voters under 40 on the go need to see that Ed Markey willfully doesn’t understand AI and is clinging to power while AI companies go unregulated, destroying our planet, our jobs and our mental health…. [They] need to see that Seth Moulton is a next generation progressive fighter who supports abolishing ICE, taxing the rich and health care for all.”

If that sort of appeal comes off as desperate opportunism, that’s because it is. Just last year, Moulton told The Boston Globe that progressive populism is “great for Democrats if we want to continue losing.” Jonathan Cohn, policy director of Progressive Mass, denounced Moulton’s 2026 moves. “Seth has done a fascinating job of trying to rebrand himself as progressive this cycle,” Cohn told The Lever. “[Moulton] doesn’t ever really actually hit on the big problem over the past few decades of the Democratic Party’s movement away from thinking about how the government can positively intervene to improve people’s everyday lives.”

Markey’s victory surprised some people, but I wasn’t one of them. I have never considered Moulton any kind of progressive, and I remember when Markey beat former representative Joseph P. Kennedy III, scion of Massachusetts’s most powerful political dynasty. No member of the Kennedy clan had ever lost a race there before. In November, Markey faces Republican John Deaton, who in 2024 lost badly to Elizabeth Warren.

fullText:
BATON ROUGE, La. (Louisiana First) -- A longtime Baton Rouge high school football rivalry returns this week as McKinley and Capitol prepare to battle for bragging rights in the third annual "Downtown Showdown."

Before the teams meet on the field, players, coaches and administrators from both schools will come together Wednesday for a joint press conference to preview the matchup.

The press conference is scheduled for 5:30 p.m. Wednesday, Sept. 2, at the McKinley Alumni Center, located at 1520 Thomas Delpit Drive.

The Downtown Showdown kicks off at 7 p.m. Thursday, Sept. 3, at Memorial Stadium.

EBR Schools said McKinley enters this year's game looking to keep the Downtown Showdown trophy for a third straight season. The Panthers narrowly defeated Capitol 20-18 last year.

The rivalry between the two schools dates back to 1950. McKinley and Capitol played annually until 2019 before reviving the series in 2024 with a trophy and bragging rights on the line.

Despite McKinley's recent wins, Capitol holds the advantage in the historic rivalry, leading the all-time series 37-34-3.

Louisiana First News will stream the press conference live in the video player above.

title: Barcelona new signing trains by himself at club facilities, could debut vs Valencia
description: According to Mundo Deportivo, FC Barcelona deadline-day signing Gabriel Jesus took part in an individual training session at the Ciutat Esportiva Joan Gamper today.Indeed, the Brazilian forward traine...
fullText:
According to Mundo Deportivo, FC Barcelona deadline-day signing Gabriel Jesus took part in an individual training session at the Ciutat Esportiva Joan Gamper today.

Indeed, the Brazilian forward trained individually at the club facilities, as the rest of the squad did not hold a joint training session on Wednesday.

He is expected to train with his new teammates for the first time on Thursday, when he should also get his first opportunity to work on the pitch with a ball.

The report further states that Jesus is expected to be included in the squad for Barcelona's fourth La Liga fixture of the season, when Hansi Flick's side travel to face Valencia at Mestalla.

It could potentially be where the 29-year-old striker makes his first appearance in the Blaugrana shirt, although the final decision will be up to manager Hansi Flick.

New Barcelona player. (Picture credit: X/@FCBarcelona)

The Brazilian arrives after completing pre-season under Mikel Arteta at Arsenal, featuring in three matches without completing 90 minutes in any of them.

His only pre-season goal came in the Trofeu Costa Brava, when Arsenal faced Girona at Montilivi.

Jesus returned to action in December 2025 after recovering from a cruciate ligament injury that had kept him out for almost a year.

As the second half of last season progressed, the Brazilian gradually regained his rhythm. Arsenal ultimately went on to win the Premier League and reached the Champions League final where they lost to PSG.

Jesus has recovered from his ACL injury. (Photo by Justin Setterfield/Getty Images)

The 29-year-old forward did not feature in that final, but his increasing involvement during the latter stages of the campaign means he arrives at Barcelona fully recovered from his previous injury problems.

Barcelona signed Jesus for €10 million in fixed payments plus a further €4 million in variables. He has signed a three-year contract with the Catalan capital until 2029.

Having had his first training session with the club today, Jesus could make his maiden appearance in the Blaugrana colours this weekend when they take on Valencia, provided Flick considers him to be ready.

title: 'There are no exceptions': Judge forbids Tiger Woods from driving for 5 years
description: Golfer Tiger Woods pleaded guilty to lesser charges of reckless driving after he was initially charged with DUI following a crash.
fullText:
STUART, Fla. (Court TV) — Tiger Woods will have to limit his driving to the golf course after he pleaded no contest to charges following a crash in Florida.

Woods, 50, entered the plea to amended charges six months after he rolled his SUV on Jupiter Island. Investigators said the pro golfer was illegally trying to pass a truck hauling a trailer; when Woods passed the truck, his Land Rover left the road and flipped onto its side. Nobody was hurt.

Prosecutors initially charged Woods with driving under the influence and refusing to submit to testing; on Wednesday, he entered pleas to charges of reckless driving and careless driving.

"Since I initially filed on these charges, there's been a very significant erosion of evidence," Assistant State Attorney Nirlaine Smart said Wednesday morning at Woods' change-of-plea hearing.

Outside the courtroom, State Attorney Thomas Bakkedahl held a news conference to explain why prosecutors agreed to amend the charges. "This case turned out to be a particularly difficult DUI to prove," he said.

Neither side disputed the basic facts of the case: Woods had been driving the SUV when it crashed on March 27, 2026. At the scene, Woods denied drinking alcohol, but told deputies, "I took a few," in reference to medications; deputies found two hydrocodone pills in his pocket.

Bakkedahl said that sobriety tests deputies administered at the crash scene were unreliable because of Woods' documented history of back and leg surgeries, which have left his gait unsteady. The defendant also refused a drug screening, so "we don't know exactly what was in his bloodstream at the time," Bakkedahl said.

Prosecutors subpoenaed Woods' medical and prescription records, which revealed that he had a valid prescription for the medication in his pocket. Woods also gave investigators access to the Land Rover without a warrant, but the manufacturer refused to cooperate further and provide access to the vehicle's black box.

Ultimately, Bakkedahl said he decided to amend the charges after two toxicologists hired to review the case "were of the opinion that there was insufficient proof" to establish that Woods was under the influence at the time of the crash.

Under the plea agreement, Woods will not serve jail time but must pay a $1,000 fine. His driver's license will also be suspended for five years.

"Sir, I want you to understand that five years of driving is for the safety of the public," Judge Darren Steele warned. "There are no exceptions. If you were to drive for any reason at all, you would go immediately back to jail."

Woods was previously cited in 2023 in California for a crash caused by excessive speed; he was also cited in 2009 for careless driving after hitting a fire hydrant and a tree in Florida.

title: Kyle Van Noy has a new team for his 13th NFL season
description: It’s been an eventful past week for Kyle Van Noy.  Just a few days after he was announced as a new inductee into the BYU Athletic Hall of Fame, Van Noy signed with the Minnesota Vikings for his 13th NFL season, according to a Tuesday report from Tom Pelissero of The Ringer.  Veteran OLB Kyle Van Noy is signing with the Vikings, sources tell @ringer @netflixsports.
fullText:
It's been an eventful past week for Kyle Van Noy.

Just a few days after he was announced as a new inductee into the BYU Athletic Hall of Fame, Van Noy signed with the Minnesota Vikings for his 13th NFL season, according to a Tuesday report from Tom Pelissero of The Ringer.

Veteran OLB Kyle Van Noy is signing with the Vikings, sources tell @ringer @netflixsports. 

Van Noy and DC Brian Flores won two Super Bowls together with the Patriots. Now they’re teaming up in Minnesota, where Van Noy will start on the practice squad to ramp up. pic.twitter.com/VPyL4aosTD

As reported by Pelissero, Van Noy will begin his Minnesota tenure on the team's practice squad to "ramp up" for game action after missing all of training camp.

Van Noy spent the past three years with the Baltimore Ravens, where he posted the two highest single-season sack totals of his career (nine in 2023, 12.5 in 2024) and made the 2024 Pro Bowl.

In 173 NFL contests with the Ravens, New England Patriots, Miami Dolphins, Los Angeles Chargers and Detroit Lions, Van Noy has recorded 57 sacks (the most for any BYU alum) with 14 forced fumbles, four interceptions and three defensive touchdowns.

Van Noy, who won two Super Bowls with the Patriots, now reunites in Minnesota with Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores, who was Van Noy's linebackers coach in New England.

Arguably the most dominant defensive player in program history, Van Noy's BYU career included 25 sacks, 61.5 tackles for loss, seven interceptions, 11 forced fumbles and five touchdowns.

The match officials for Saturday's Premier League meeting with Brighton have been announced, with Stuart Attwell set to take charge at the Amex.

The 43-year-old began the new campaign with a UEFA Conference League Qualifying tie between Qarabağ and Dynamo Kyiv before overseeing the dramatic late draw between Newcastle United and Liverpool on the Premier League's opening weekend.

Vastly experienced at the top of the game, Attwell has refereed 244 Premier League games and was in the middle for the 2025 FA Cup Final.

The Whites have a mixed record from their 25 fixtures to involve Attwell, winning 12 of those and drawing on three occasions. Three of those fixtures came last term, including a memorable 2-1 home victory over West Ham United at Elland Road that brought goals from Brenden Aaronson and Joe Rodon.

Brighton, meanwhile, have won 13 of 31 matches officiated by the Warwickshire-based referee, losing 10 times. Most recently, the Seagulls drew 2-2 with Tottenham towards the end of the previous season.

title: Warriors' Jimmy Butler gets eye-opening trade update from ESPN analyst coming off ACL injury
description: The Golden State Warriors have enjoyed having Jimmy Butler over the last couple of seasons. However, there is belief his name will come up at the trade deadline.
fullText:
Warriors' Jimmy Butler gets eye-opening trade update from ESPN analyst coming off ACL injury originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The Golden State Warriors are likely to have an up-and-down season this year, no matter how you look at it. The team could struggle early without Jimmy Butler, as he continues to work his way back from injury.

The Warriors lost Butler last season against the Miami Heat, and he ultimately required surgery on his torn ACL.

"Injured Golden State Warriors star Jimmy Butler underwent successful surgery on his torn right ACL on Monday morning in Los Angeles, the team announced," ESPN's Anthony Slater wrote. "Butler suffered the injury on Jan. 19 in a win over the Miami Heat. He consulted several specialists for the surgery, landing on Dr. Bert Mandelbaum, who performed it on Monday morning with a few members of the Warriors' organization on hand."

There is no official timeline for Butler's return, but there is hope that he will be back before the trade deadline.

"If Butler can get back on the floor before the trade deadline, which appears very likely at the moment, this organization will be able to figure out their plan heading into the trade madness and what their playoff outlook is," NBA insider Brett Siegel wrote.

If the Warriors struggle to find success this season, Butler could become an intriguing trade piece. ESPN's Brian Windhorst recently explained why Butler's expiring contract could make him attractive to other teams.

"I know there's been a whole bunch of discussion dating back to last trade deadline about Jimmy Butler. Him coming off the ACL he could function as a huge expiring contract in a trade. I don't think they're operating with day to day. But if player/acquisition comes to the four, they could use that," Windhorst wrote.

Steph Curry and Draymond Green have clearly enjoyed playing with Butler and appreciate what he brings to the team. However, if Golden State can land significant talent in return and use that haul to build around Curry for the final stages of his career, it could be a move worth considering.

Butler would be a valuable piece for any contender, but the possibility of acquiring a strong collection of talent in return could make the Warriors more willing to part ways with him. His future in the Bay Area will be something to monitor closely as the season progresses.

title: Lions 'still have confidence' Kerby Joseph, Brian Branch will return
description: General manager Brad Holmes on Wednesday, Sept. 2, said the Lions "still have confidence" both Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch will return to the field.
fullText:
ALLEN PARK — Detroit Lions safeties Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch are both starting the season on the reserve/Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list, meaning they'll be sidelined for at least the first four games of 2026.

But hope remains within the Lions regarding their potential returns.

"We still have confidence that they can come back, we just can't really give an exact timeline," Lions general manager Brad Holmes said Wednesday, Sept. 2. "They're both here, they're rehabbing, they're working hard. Just can't offer a timeline. But yeah, the hope is to have both of them back at some point."

Joseph has been dealing with a knee injury since at least last summer, when he missed time in training camp. Joseph went on to make six appearances for the Lions in 2025, with his last coming in a loss to the Kansas City Chiefs on Oct. 12. There was hope Joseph could get back on the field at some point last season, but he ultimately was placed on injured reserve Dec. 20, ending his fourth campaign.

Branch, meanwhile, tore his Achilles against the Dallas Cowboys on Dec. 4. In July, Lions coach Dan Campbell said Branch could begin practicing in late August or early September, and he said Joseph was "on the Branch plan a little bit, and that's if everything goes well and everything goes according to plan with him and we've got everything on our side."

Though neither Branch nor Joseph will be eligible to play play in a game until Detroit's Week 5 contest at the Arizona Cardinals on Oct. 11, both can return to practice as early as Sept. 18, one day after the Lions' Week 2 game at the Buffalo Bills.

The Lions plan to start Chuck Clark and Avonte Maddox at safety to begin the season, with Thomas Harper providing depth at the position. Aamaris Brown, a versatile defensive back who signed with the Lions as an undrafted free agent, is on the practice squad.

This article originally appeared on The Detroit News: Lions 'still have confidence' Kerby Joseph, Brian Branch will return

In the preseason, they finished 2-1, with double-digit wins over the Seattle Seahawks and Arizona Cardinals.After a successful five weeks of training camp and […] The post Cowboys’ ‘Solid Summer’ Led to Passing Grade in Preseason appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
From Day 1 of training camp, the Dallas Cowboys looked like a completely different team.

The Cowboys had strong practices and were competitive against the Los Angeles Rams in their joint practice. In the preseason, they finished 2-1, with double-digit wins over the Seattle Seahawks and Arizona Cardinals.

After a successful five weeks of training camp and preseason games, the Cowboys appear to be one of the biggest winners so far in the NFL. They got that vindication with a single grade.

CBS Sports writer Tyler Sullivan gave every NFL team grades on how they did in 2026. Sullivan gave the Cowboys a B+.

"Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb, and a number of other key Cowboys starters didn't partake in the preseason. That said, there was plenty of intrigue on the offensive side of the ball as Sam Howell and Joe Milton duked it out for the backup role. Howell won out, with Milton being waived. On defense, third-round linebacker Jaishawn Barham opened eyes with his play this summer, giving Dallas some much-needed depth at the position with upside for more. Undrafted wideout Camden Brown made the opening 53-man roster after catching six balls for 166 yards and two touchdowns this preseason. Meanwhile, from a player-acquisition standpoint, the Cowboys added pass rusher Von Miller and offensive tackle Broderick Jones during the preseason. Again, the headliners that we'll see in Week 1 stayed behind the scenes, but Dallas put together a solid summer."

Dallas' offense led the charge with great passing performances from Milton and Howell, who both had over 300 yards each in three games. Even on defense, the Cowboys allowed just 20 points in their first two games against the Seahawks and Cardinals.

This team is improved in every aspect on offense, defense, and special teams. After going 7-9-1 last season, the Cowboys have the makings of a playoff team in 2026.

Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer is now in Year 2 on the job and has Christian Parker running the defense. Dallas added a ton of talent, including Von Miller and Broderick Jones, to further improve the roster in the preseason.

They still have a lot of work to do, but this franchise is finally heading in the right direction. After missing the playoffs two years in a row, it feels more realistic that they can compete for not only a playoff spot, but for the NFC East title.

A roster this deep is what the Cowboys needed to turn things around. This team is trending in the right direction.

title: Dodgers Have One Bright Spot During Poor Stretch of Play
description: The Los Angeles Dodgers have not been playing their best baseball as of late, but Mookie Betts is heating up
fullText:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have not been playing great lately, going 26-26 since the start of July 1.

A .500 record over the course of two months is not terrible, and the team still has one of the best records in baseball, but when the lineup and rotation is as good as it is, .500 feels like a let down. One of the biggest issues for the Dodgers has been that their star hitters are slumping. In fact, some have been struggling all season. Andy Pages' injury and Will Smith missing a chunk of games certainly do not help.

Smith is back now, but it will take more than just him to get the team on track. One player who has played well as of late is Mookie Betts. Betts is not having a great year overall, and his struggles are part of the reason the Dodgers have not been as dominant as expected. Betts had a .670 OPS on Aug. 4.

Since then, he has had a .304/.379/.478 slash line. He has raised his OPS to .714 and is starting to look like the superstar he is. The Dodgers will need him to stay hot through the final month and in October.

Looking for the perfect gift for a baseball player in your life? Check out our brand new baseball lifestyle brand!

Freddie Freeman has been good all year, and Shohei Ohtani will likely get back to swinging a hot bat very soon. When those two and Betts are going right, the Dodgers already know they can win the World Series.

Their starting rotation is expected to be the best in the postseason, so all they really need is for the offense to break out of an extended slump. Betts' resurgence is a great sign for the Dodgers offense and should give fans hope that the team could start dominating again soon.

Their offense scored the sixth fewest runs in baseball in August, and they went 13-14 in the month. That is certainly not the standard the team has set, and they will need the stars to step up if they want to go on another World Series run.

title: College coaches name Michigan football top sleeper team for 2026
description: College coaches are naming Michigan football as a top sleeper team this season under new coach Kyle Whittingham.
fullText:
There aren't many expecting Michigan football to make major waves this season, but there are some who think that the Wolverines may be better than a lot of people are expecting. And among them are college coaches.

With Kyle Whittingham taking over the program after a successful 21-year head coaching stint at Utah, there are hopes in Ann Arbor that his ability to get more out of less in Salt Lake City will translate to him getting more out of more at The Big House. And given that this might be the most talent he's ever worked with, it's an intriguing prospect that he could make a big impact right away.

The Athletic polled coaches anonymously across college football, and though there weren't the highest of expectations for the maize and blue, Michigan topped the entire landscape with three votes from coaches indicating that the Wolverines could be the biggest sleeper in the country.

One coach off the record oversees tight ends in the American Conference, and another was an offensive line coach from the Mountain West.

"I really want to see what Whittingham does at Michigan. They're so creative in the run game. I wouldn't be shocked if you blinked and they're 10-2." — American Conference tight ends coach

"I could see him with some of those Michigan guys with the Utah culture make them really good, really good fast. They have an identity, and it's the type of identity that they've wanted there." — Mountain West offensive line coach

Yes, the schedule is an absolute bear, but there's a reason why teams play the games -- because often preseason expectations don't equal regular season results. So while we can look at Oklahoma, Iowa, Penn State, Indiana, Oregon, and Ohio State on the schedule as a daunting slate, any of them could be worse than expectations, in concert with Michigan actually being better than expected. Last year, Penn State and Clemson were considered top-five teams in the preseason, and both finished unranked. LSU often starts in the top 10 and has struggled mightily since winning the national championship following the 2019 season.

But then there's the case of 2021 Michigan. The Wolverines were much better than anyone anticipated that year, having gone 11-1 that year, beating what was considered to be among the best Ohio State teams in recent history, 42-27, at The Big House. Could 2026 be a reprise of 2021? Given that this is a reset under Whittingham, and the team reportedly has solid player-led leadership, it could mirror that season perhaps -- though the road to Indianapolis and beyond is certainly much tougher than it appeared to be that year.
