fullText:
As Rockstar’s blockbuster prepares to dominate the headlines, it’s time for the mainstream media to stop treating video games as a novelty that needs explaining

Predictably, the Grand Theft Auto VI “extended look” which premiered on Netflix last week was a success for all involved. The 30-minute preview scorched to No 1 on the viewing chart and even brought the site down for a few minutes as millions of gamers tried to watch what was, effectively, a very long teaser trailer. According to data collated by Eurogamer, more than 9,000 Twitch streamers covered the show leading to 5,227,798 hours of viewing there alone. And this was just the beginning of what will surely be two months of escalating hype – and unprecedented media attention.

Call me cynical, but I suspect the coverage of GTA VI in the media over the next few weeks will follow a familiar pattern. Mostly, it will be five-minute slots wedged in near the end of news bulletins in which games journalists, industry analysts and other pundits will be asked why the game is such a big deal, how much it cost to make and how much revenue it will generate. Perhaps a few will try to reignite the hoary old “violence in video games” debate, there will be presenters laughingly admitting they’ve not touched a game since Pac-Man, rolling their eyes and wallowing in their ignorance, in a way they never would while discussing any other art form. Somebody will venture the subversive view that “games are no longer just for kids”; somebody else will say “games make more money than films and music put together”. And that will be that, job done for another decade … or until there’s a funny story about Pokémon.

I hope I’m wrong. I hope, at least, the BBC, which employs plenty of staff who understand video games, will make time in its schedule to take a good look at GTA VI – its themes and influences, its creators, its place in the wider culture of games and entertainment. Sure, arts coverage on BBC television has been in decline for years, with the broadcaster shifting this content to digital platforms, but I saw plenty of in-depth analysis of Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey, looking at the quality of its translation, its depiction of female characters, its use of practical effects. I didn’t see a single presenter shrugging, looking comedically bewildered and admitting they’d not read Homer since secondary school.

On top of this, whatever mainstream media attention GTA VI does get it will come at the expense of covering other titles. Because, when the next video game story comes up in the wake of Rockstar’s behemoth, TV and radio editors and producers will be thinking, “Oh, we covered games last month.”

The thing is, GTA is a phenomenon – it looks gorgeous, it looks vast, and it will sell many millions of copies. The series’ notoriety transcends the medium. But is it the most interesting video game since GTA V? So much has changed since then. We’ve explored the fascinating, innovative open worlds of Elden Ring, Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and No Man’s Sky (an open galaxy!); we’ve seen brutal adult themes explored in The Last of Us: Part 2 and Silent Hill; we’ve experienced dizzying narrative innovations via Disco Elysium, Split Fiction and Lost Records: Bloom & Rage. All of these deserved at least a portion of that GTA screen and radio time.

True, some games have drawn similar levels of media attention. Minecraft and Fortnite receive regular coverage, but almost always because of concerns over children and games addiction, or because of how they intersect with other media: Minecraft through its hit movie, Fortnite through its many collaborations with music artists. And this is the key problem. Mainstream media is still at the stage where every single games story that does make it to TV or radio has to do the job of explaining and justifying the whole industry. It’s time for programme-makers to understand that video games are a mass cultural phenomenon. Enough people play them and understand them so that they don’t have to be re-introduced every time they’re covered. And most importantly, there is life, love, art and brilliance beyond Grand Theft Auto and beyond the coming storm of hype.

It was my birthday a couple of weeks ago, so I set out to find a simple, fun video game that the whole family could enjoy – and I wanted to share my discovery.

Inspired by Dominik Diamond’s recent column on this very subject, I downloaded the party game What The Dub?!, in which players watch old film clips with portions of the sound dubbed out and then enter their own amusing dialogue to fill the gap. The clips are then re-shown with each player’s text added to the soundtrack via a stilted robotic voice – then everyone votes on the funniest entry. It was hilarious, especially because the clips are from weird old public domain films and TV shows, so everything feels stilted and ridiculous. It’s also simple to take part, with each player using their phone to enter their dialogue choices. Apparently, it’s possible to add new clips via the Steam Workshop, the digital store’s user-generated content feature, but we didn’t figure that out. Regardless, What the Dub?! will definitely be revived at future family celebrations.

Available on: PC

 Estimated playtime: All evening!

EA staff have been speaking anonymously to the industry-news site Game Developer about their concerns after the Saudi-led buyout of Electronic Arts. Some are troubled by the prospect of popular games such as EA Sports FC, Madden and Battlefield being used by Saudi Arabia to distract from its poor human rights record. There are also worries about the company’s culture and job security.

TV producers looking for interesting game stories that don’t involve GTA could check out Eurogamer’s excellent article on the No Man’s Sky’s Galactic Hub project. It’s a community of players exploring and scientifically cataloguing specific regions of the long-running space adventure sim, like a sort of ragtag Starfleet mission. Live long and prosper, lads.

As if making and marketing independent video games isn’t hard enough, several developers have reported thefts at this year’s Gamescom event in Cologne. Posting on X, Mimic creator Ryan Laley said: “Our equipment was stolen last night from the booth. Police reports have been filed. At a loss for words to describe the feeling. Just defeated. Gonna do my best with what’s left of the week. But a huge blow financially and mentally.” According to VGC, others affected included publisher iam8bit and Tessera Studios.

Star Wars Zero Company – joyfully absurd heroics with a tight-knit team of misfits | ★★★★☆

Vholume – a headlong rush of parkour perfection in a brutalist wonderland | ★★★★☆

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy – picture-postcard retelling of haunting Minoan myth | ★★★☆☆

A question from Richard via email:

“My son, aged 6, is a big fan of aeroplanes and is really interested in flight. What games are there that could be used to entertain him, as a thing to do with me. I have (ridiculously) a PS5 and Xbox Series X – is Flight Simulator right? How about Ace Combat? Anything else?”

I’d definitely recommend Microsoft Flight Simulator, which is available on PS5 and Xbox. It can be controlled with just a joypad and you can switch off all the technical elements for your son so he’s basically just steering the craft like in an arcade game. There are lots of aircraft to fly, from tiny prop planes to passenger jets, and you can choose anywhere on Earth to explore. I love simply zooming over cities and scenic highlights, taking it all in.

If you’re ok with him doing a bit of shooting, Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve is out in October, promising highly detailed visuals and exciting dogfighting. Fans say it looks to be a highlight for the series. I’d also recommend No Man’s Sky, which is a space exploration game, but the flight feels lovely, whether you’re scorching over the surface of a planet or out in the depths of the cosmos. The controls are extremely intuitive too. If he gets into space flight, the slightly more involved Elite Dangerous is worth a look, and for an accessible combination of space flight and shooting, Everspace: Stellar Edition is a really nice option on PS5.

If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us at pushingbuttons@theguardian.com.

title: The best kettles in the UK to save energy and speed up your cuppa, tested
description:
We boiled litres of water to find the best electric kettles, from hard-water heroes to vintage-style, repairable and wifi-connected models
• The best air fryers, tried and tested for crisp and crunch
Despite the march of progress, the humble kettle remains a kitchen staple. It’s what we turn to in times of strife, when spirits are flagging, or to start our day. When a visitor calls, one of the first things we often do is put the kettle on.
Many small appliances have evolved beyond their original form, but the kettle’s basic principles remain largely unchanged. Water goes in and heats until a thermostat switches it off; the water then pours out, and we enjoy a cuppa.
fullText:
We boiled litres of water to find the best electric kettles, from hard-water heroes to vintage-style, repairable and wifi-connected models

The best air fryers, tried and tested for crisp and crunch

Despite the march of progress, the humble kettle remains a kitchen staple. It’s what we turn to in times of strife, when spirits are flagging, or to start our day. When a visitor calls, one of the first things we often do is put the kettle on.

Many small appliances have evolved beyond their original form, but the kettle’s basic principles remain largely unchanged. Water goes in and heats until a thermostat switches it off; the water then pours out, and we enjoy a cuppa. However, the technology that goes into a kettle has been slowly improving: better insulation to keep water hotter for longer and reduce reboils; different temperature settings to suit every drink from green tea to herbal brews; and more features such as filters and concealed elements to keep scale out of our cups.

When your existing kettle makes its last brew and must be taken to the big recycling centre in the sky, it pays to check out what’s on offer to replace it. The next one you buy may make more of a difference to your day than you might think.

Best kettle overall
Bosch Sky kettle

Best budget kettle
Kenwood Ripple kettle

The forever kettle
Dualit Classic kettle

The fastest-boiling kettle
Ninja Perfect Temperature kettle

Best budget variable temperature kettle
Lakeland Digital double-walled kettle

When a friend heard I was writing this, she asked me, “Aren’t all kettles the same? They all boil water, don’t they?” And while she’s right about the second part, it took me at least 15 minutes to explain why she was wrong about the first. I’ve been testing kettles for years, and they vary greatly – in design, weight, ease of maintenance, ease of use and build quality. Some will last for decades while others will barely make it past the basic guarantee period. In short, yes, all kettles boil water – but they are far from being all the same.

As you can imagine, I boiled a lot of water. Litres upon litres of the stuff. Enough to turn my kitchen into the steamiest hammam and clear my pores of blackheads I’ve had since I was a teenager.

Testing wasn’t just about making gallons of tea and having a deep skin cleanse on the cheap, though. I also brought a lot of gadgets to the party: a power meter to assess electricity use for each kettle when boiling exactly one litre of water from cold; a timer to measure how long that took; and a probe thermometer to gauge how long it took for the kettle to click off once it had reached boiling point.

External temperature was measured using an infrared thermometer and the highest reading noted, while maximum noise levels were recorded with the Decibel X app. After boiling, water temperature was checked at the 30-minute, one- and two-hour points to see how much it had cooled.

I tested 13 kettles in total. The ones that made the cut were selected on the basis of good energy efficiency or low minimum fill, plus ease of use or maintenance. Value for money has also been considered, as have longer guarantees and durable build quality that should translate into a lengthy lifespan for the appliance. Energy costs below have been calculated based on the 1 October to 31 December 2026 price cap in Great Britain. All samples have been returned to their supplier or donated to Caterham Round Table to raise funds for local causes and charity projects.

Offering variable temperatures and a double-walled stainless-steel housing, the 3kW Sky is a brilliant blend of robust form and function. It boasts a low minimum boil (300ml, which is just over a cup), a keep-warm setting and touch controls.

Why we love it
I found it difficult to select a best kettle from so many that performed well, but the Bosch Sky clinched it because it’s such a good all-rounder that will suit most people. It pours well, has a button that’s within easy reach of the handle so it’s simple to open the lid without touching it, and it’s insulated so the exterior doesn’t become too hot to touch. From a design perspective, it has a more industrial feel than many others – no frippery here – but not too modern that it wouldn’t fit into most kitchens. Its display is thoughtfully designed, easy to keep clean and lights up as it heats.

The exterior doesn’t get too hot (up to 40C), and while it wasn’t the fastest to boil in testing, it was only seconds behind the Dualit below. It clicked off at boiling point, and the water was still a toasty 78C 30 minutes later. At the hour point, it was 66C, and after two hours 52C, meaning you’ll spend less time and energy reboiling.

It’s a shame that … its premium look ends at the handle, which seems cheap and plasticky next to the sleek aesthetic of the rest of it.

Although it comes with a higher initial outlay, Dualit’s Classic kettle is more of a “buy right, buy once” appliance. It’s as robust as they come, with a durable stainless-steel body, hinged lid, anti-wobble feet and non-drip spout. But it’s the repairable nature of this kettle that makes it an eco-friendly buy. The 3kW element is replaceable, so a pro can swap it for a new one or repair it if it wears out, meaning you may never need to buy a new kettle again.

Why we love it
Repairability aside, the Dualit Classic kettle also makes it easy to boil only as much water as you need, with a low minimum fill (250ml) and dual water windows indicating cups and litres via multiple markings. There’s no button to raise the lid, meaning one less thing to go wrong; instead, it has a heatproof plastic handle. It was also the second fastest boiling of all the kettles tested and clicked off bang on boiling point.

It’s a shame that … the exterior gets hot after boiling – our sample reached 71C. It also lacked a choice of temperatures and a keep-warm function, despite the higher price.

As you’d expect from Ninja, this kettle has features galore, right down to the same familiar beep all Ninja appliances use when you turn them on. However, most notable is its “hold temp”, which keeps your water at a selected temperature for up to half an hour – great for the easily distracted and busy households alike.

Why we love it
Out of all the kettles tested, this was the fastest, boiling its litre in just over two minutes with its 3kW element. Also in its favour is a 250ml minimum fill, although this is only shown on the inside of the kettle, not the outside. Both cups and litres are denoted in multiple increments on its water window, so there’s little chance of boiling more than you need. It also uses the least energy of any kettle on test.

The six different temperatures each has its own button, meaning no need to scroll until you reach your desired heat. The only place it came unstuck was a lack of insulation. Heat was retained for the first 30 minutes (72C) and hour (58C), but its two-hour temperature was 43C.

It’s a shame that … the exterior becomes hot: the meter registered a temperature of 97C just before boiling. Plus, it took a couple of seconds to click off once 100C had been reached.

Lakeland’s digital double-walled kettle proves you don’t have to splash the cash for a well-insulated, variable temperature kettle – or one with a decent warranty length. With a powerful 3kW element, a wide choice of temperatures and a keep-warm setting, plus easy controls, it’s hard to ask for more at this price.

Why we love it
What impressed me most about this kettle, aside from its choice of 13 temperatures, was its large, clear display. The double-walled construction served it well: the exterior reached only 27C, while the water was still 78C after 30 minutes, dropping to 67C after an hour and 53C after two hours. However, it did take a couple of seconds to click off after boiling.

This wifi-connected kettle won’t be for everyone, but it may appeal to those who, hands full with kids or shopping, would like Alexa to put on the kettle for them. Beyond its smart features, it’s a decent kettle, using second lowest energy of those tested and letting you easily set different temperatures. It didn’t make the final cut because … its 1.8kW element meant it was slow to boil, and it took about six seconds to click off after reaching boiling point. The display is difficult to read in bright light, and there’s a 500ml minimum fill, with no markings between that and the max fill.

Instantly recognisable, Smeg’s 50s-style kettle has a vintage aesthetic that has won it a legion of fans. However, there’s no getting away from the fact that it’s one of the priciest while not offering much more than the others. The good stuff: it’s stylish, has excellent build quality and a 3kW element that boiled fast. Best for: an affordable luxury kettle

If the price of the two stylish kettles above has you wincing, fear not: you can bag an attractive kettle for less than £30. Enter Tower’s Scandi kettle, available in several shades, all of which have faux wood and chrome-effect detailing. There’s good stuff besides the design, too: it’s lightweight (940g), has a speedy boiling 3kW element, and water windows on both sides that are marked with cups and litres.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the minimum fill is 500ml, and it took six seconds to click off after reaching 100C. It’s also not very well insulated: the exterior reached 84C after boiling, and while the water temperature was 72C 30 minutes after boiling, it registered at only 44C two hours later.

Time to boil one litre: 2mins 21secs; minimum fill: 500mll; maximum fill: 1.7l; dimensions: 16.5 x 25.5 x 24cm (WDH); total weight: 0.9kg; power use: 0.117kWh = 3p at 26.32p per kWh; matching toaster? Yes; maximum noise recorded: 59dB; temperature settings: 100C; warranty: one year

How you use your kettle will probably dictate which functions you’ll find the most useful, but generally, any feature that helps to save energy is valuable. For example, kettles that are dual-walled help to trap heat inside, so the water stays warmer for longer while the outside stays cool to the touch.

Those with low minimum fills enable you to boil just enough water for a single cup, so you don’t waste energy heating more than you need. Some kettles also have a keep-warm function that stops the water cooling below a certain temperature, which is ideal for those who become distracted after boiling or drink consecutive cuppas. It’s a good idea to check for safety features too, such as an auto shut-off to prevent it from boiling dry if there’s not enough water.

Other features are more “nice to haves”: variable temperature models enable you to choose water heated to lower temperatures than boiling, such as 70C or 80C, for other types of tea or for filling a hot-water bottle. Concealed elements, which are easier to keep scale-free, and removable, washable limescale filters will be useful for those who live in hard-water areas. Then there’s connectivity. While wifi-enabled and voice-controlled kettles can feel a little gimmicky, they can be a gift for busy parents who usually have their hands full.

Rapid-boil kettles don’t have a strict industry definition, so while a rapid-boil kettle should boil water quickly, it may not differ much from one that’s not labelled as such.

A more reliable indicator of how fast a kettle will boil is its power rating: this is listed either in watts (eg 3,000W) or kilowatts (eg 2.2kW). The higher the number, the more power its element can use to heat water quickly. However, this isn’t the whole story: boiling times can also be quicker in double-walled kettles (as they lose less heat to their surroundings) and those with concealed or flat elements (which provide more surface area to heat the water than a coil).

Limescale reduces your kettle’s efficiency, costing you more to boil each time, and shortening the appliance’s lifespan. Descale it monthly, especially if you live in a hard-water area. Standing water encourages the buildup of limescale, so try not to leave water in the kettle after use.

While you can buy descaler in the supermarket, a lower-cost and more eco-friendly option is to combine a weak food-safe acid, such as white vinegar or lemon juice, with water. Fill the kettle three-quarters with either water and the juice of one lemon or equal parts water and vinegar. Let it soak for an hour, then boil the kettle (once for vinegar, three times for lemon). Once it’s cooled, rinse thoroughly. If your kettle has a removable filter, take it out and rinse it under running water at the same time.

The material a kettle’s body and lid are made from can make a difference to the appliance’s durability, daily use and even the taste of your drink. The most common materials for electric kettles are plastic, stainless steel and glass.

Plastic is probably the one you’ll encounter the most. It allows kettles to be affordable, lightweight – crucial if you have difficulty lifting or pouring when it’s full – and can be almost any colour or texture.

Over time, though, plastic can be prone to damage, such as cracks or scratches, and can absorb odours. This means a plastic kettle will usually need to be replaced more frequently than others. Most modern models are made using food-grade plastic, are BPA-free (check websites and labels to be sure), and meet current safety standards: research remains inconclusive about health risks from using a plastic kettle.

Stainless steel is another popular material for kettles. It’s hard-wearing, hygienic and resistant to corrosion, scratches and damage. Stainless steel is also a recyclable material (although the recyclability of your kettle will also depend on its construction and how easily its different materials can be separated). In terms of everyday use, good-quality stainless steel is considered to be taste neutral (although a new kettle may impart a slight metallic flavour at first).

Kettles made from stainless steel tend to be heavier overall, and will become hot on the outside when boiling and for some time afterwards. They may also be louder when boiling and can stain over time.

Glass kettles have been steadily gaining in popularity – for many, watching the bubbles rise during a boil is part of the ritual. Taste-neutral – a must for tea lovers who want their blends to shine – glass kettles are usually made from borosilicate glass, just like the glassware in laboratories, which is resistant to thermal shock and rapid temperature changes. The material is also non-toxic, non-reactive and won’t corrode – plus, you can always see how much water is left.

A glass kettle tends to be heavier than plastic but lighter than stainless steel. However, while glass kettles are tough enough to withstand daily use, they can still break on impact. You may also find they don’t retain heat as well as other materials, and if you live in a hard-water area, the visible limescale may lead to a more frequent need for descaling.

According to various estimates, the average kettle lasts around six to eight years. The higher quality the kettle, the better you maintain it and how often you use it will all determine its lifespan.

However, while this is a general guide, you should stop using your kettle if you notice damage, discoloration, leaks or any electrical safety issues – such as burning smells, rattling or buzzing sounds, scorch marks, sparks or exposed wires. A kettle that trips your electrics should be replaced immediately. Contact the manufacturer if you are still within warranty or to explore repairability options.

Performance issues are also a sign that your kettle is failing. These can include a kettle that’s taking longer to boil, or that switches off before boiling point is reached (indicative of a faulty thermostat). Even if everything looks fine inside, if water begins to taste different, looks cloudy or has a smell, it’s time for a new kettle. Limescale that is hard to shift is another sign your kettle has to go: this points to deteriorating surfaces.

If the kettle still works, some charities accept unwanted electrical items as donations, or you could give it to a friend. Some kettles can be repaired by the manufacturer, such as the Dualit model reviewed above, or repaired locally, so check if there’s a repair cafe or other repair resource near you.

If your kettle is broken or past its best, recycling is the best option. Take it to a recycling centre, drop-off point or a store that offers a retailer take-back scheme if you’re buying a new one. Your council may also be able to pick it up at the kerbside. Use the postcode checker at Recycle Your Electricals to find your nearest options.

Rachel Ogden has worked as a consumer journalist for decades, becoming an expert unboxer before it was a thing, although she’s much less adept at repacking. Her home has hosted hundreds of small appliances, from kettles and toasters to robot vacuums. When outside, you’ll find her messing about with pizza ovens, barbecues and heaters. It takes a lot to impress her – many appliances have tried and failed

title: Architect of UK’s AI strategy joins Anthropic amid conflict of interest warning
description:
Matt Clifford will stay as chair of government funding body for tech projects alongside his senior role at US firm
The architect of the UK government’s AI strategy has joined the US startup Anthropic in a senior role a year after stepping down from his Downing Street post.
Matt Clifford, a successful tech investor, was appointed as AI opportunities adviser by Keir Starmer last year but resigned from the unpaid role six months later for personal reasons.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Matt Clifford will stay as chair of government funding body for tech projects alongside his senior role at US firm

The architect of the UK government’s AI strategy has joined the US startup Anthropic in a senior role a year after stepping down from his Downing Street post.

Matt Clifford, a successful tech investor, was appointed as AI opportunities adviser by Keir Starmer last year but resigned from the unpaid role six months later for personal reasons.

His move to the company behind the Claude chatbot has raised concern, with the head of the House of Commons science, innovation and technology committee, Chi Onwurah, saying that his decision to remain as chair of the government-backed Aria funding body represented a “clear conflict of interest”.

Clifford will be Anthropic’s managing director, international affairs, and will lead the company’s engagement with governments outside the US including in the UK, Europe, Asia-Pacific and India.

Anthropic said Clifford would remain as the chair of Aria, the UK’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency, which funds “moonshot” science and tech projects. He will also maintain his chair role at Entrepreneurs First, the tech venture capital firm he co-founded.

He was appointed chair of Aria in 2022. Anthropic said Clifford would step back from any matter involving the company at Aria. But Onwurah said the roles clashed and she called on the AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, to intervene.

“His intention to remain as chair of Aria, which spends taxpayer money on cutting-edge research, much of it related to or driven by AI, is a clear conflict of interest and I look forward to the AI minister setting out clear boundaries,” Onwurah said.

Anthropic said its commercial relationship with Aria was handled by a separate team to Clifford’s and he did not make procurement or programme-level spending decision at Aria anyway.

“Matt has no involvement in any decision touching Anthropic, and that arrangement has been agreed with Aria and the Department of Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, which is responsible for appointing Aria’s chair,” the company said.

The UK government has been approached for comment.

Several senior politicians have taken roles at Silicon Valley firms in recent years. The former deputy prime minister Nick Clegg took a senior post at Meta in 2018. Last year the former prime minister Rishi Sunak took advisory roles at Microsoft and Anthropic, and the ex-chancellor George Osborne joined OpenAI.

Commenting on his role at Anthropic, Clifford said the most important decisions about AI would be made by companies and governments together. He said: “Countries everywhere want real agency over how this technology is built and used, and my job is to make Anthropic a genuine partner in that – in Europe, Asia and beyond.”

Anthropic is preparing for a stock exchange flotation that could value the business at $2tn (£1.5tn).

Tom Brake, the chief executive of Unlock Democracy, a not-for-profit campaign group, said the move showed that “the revolving door is a problem for advisers as much as it is for ministers”.

“Taking extensive knowledge obtained within government, about a policy as sensitive as AI, to a private sector company shortly after leaving government gives that company a huge advantage,” said Brake, a Liberal Democrat MP from 1997 to 2019. “Regardless of any safeguards, this weakens the government’s hand when pushing for a precautionary approach towards AI development.”

Beeban Kidron, a crossbench peer and prominent critic of the government’s AI policy, said: “We need more independent politics which puts the interests of workers, citizens and society at the forefront of our relationship with the tech sector.”

An Anthropic spokesperson said the UK was “one of dozens” of governments Clifford’s team would engage with. “We hire people with expertise and who understand how government works because our work requires it – in every market, not just the UK,” they said.

Clifford began his tech career in the private sector. Prior to his government work, he was an established figure on the UK tech scene as a co-founder of Entrepreneurs First, which has helped build tech companies with a combined worth of more than $20bn.

Clifford worked with Sunak’s government as his representative to the 2023 AI Safety Summit in the UK, and helped create the organisation that later became the world-leading AI Security Institute.

He was appointed as Starmer’s AI adviser after drafting the government’s AI action plan, which supports the creation of AI growth zones to host datacentres and the building of the UK’s own AI models.

title: Tumbler Ridge mass shooting victims file 30 new lawsuits against OpenAI
description:
The company says it prioritizes safety, but suits allege its ChatGPT bot induced  shooter to carry out attack in Canada
OpenAI faces 30 new lawsuits filed on behalf of victims of the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting.
The suits, filed on Wednesday, allege the company’s ChatGPT chatbot induced the shooter to carry out the attack in rural Canada in February, in which eight people were killed and dozens more wounded – most of them children.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
The company says it prioritizes safety, but suits allege its ChatGPT bot induced shooter to carry out attack in Canada

OpenAI faces 30 new lawsuits filed on behalf of victims of the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting.

The suits, filed on Wednesday, allege the company’s ChatGPT chatbot induced the shooter to carry out the attack in rural Canada in February, in which eight people were killed and dozens more wounded – most of them children.

“These were people who really endured just total hell that day,” Jay Edelson, the lead lawyer representing the plaintiffs, said in an interview. “Young kids who watched their teachers die, watched friends die and thought they were going to get shot and killed.”

These new lawsuits, filed in federal court for the northern district of California, come after Edelson filed seven initial suits in April – bringing the total number of cases against OpenAI for the Tumbler Ridge shooting to 37. All of the suits allege that the violent intentions of the shooter, identified as 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar, were well-known to the senior leadership of OpenAI, which failed to report her to the authorities.

Employees on the company’s safety team had flagged the shooter’s account to executives eight months before the attack, describing her in internal messages as “a credible and specific threat of gun violence against real people”, according to court filings. OpenAI banned her account, but she was able to quickly create a new one, the suits claim.

The lawsuits accuse OpenAI and its CEO, Sam Altman, of negligence, aiding and abetting a mass shooting and product liability.

Jason Kwon, OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, said in a statement that he thinks about what happened at Tumbler Ridge every day and that the company works hard to create standards for reporting cases to law enforcement.

“The professionals working on these teams choose to do this incredibly difficult work because they care so deeply about keeping people safe,” Kwon said. “They come to work every day knowing that they may have to make a decision that they’ll think about for the rest of their lives.”

A groundswell of cases have been brought against OpenAI and other tech companies alleging that their chatbots exacerbate mental health crises and provoke violent acts. OpenAI has been sued in seven separate cases that blame ChatGPT for acting as a “suicide coach”. A criminal investigation and civil lawsuit, brought by the attorney general of Florida, accuses OpenAI of concealing safety risks after a mass shooting at Florida State University.

The shooting in Tumbler Ridge took place in a secondary school, shortly after Van Rootselaar killed her mother and 11-year-old brother in their family home. The new tranche of lawsuits includes cases from the family of one girl who was shot, along with the principal, teachers and students.

The attack was one of the deadliest mass shootings in Canadian history. In the aftermath, questions swirled in the small British Columbia town about how it could have happened.

Edelson singled out Chris Lehane, who is OpenAI’s head of global affairs and a former member of Bill Clinton’s administration who specialized in opposition research. He said Lehane was one of the people who received warnings from the company’s safety team but overruled repeated appeals to alert the authorities. That decision was also sanctioned by Altman, the lawsuits allege.

“What’s clear is that OpenAI over and over has made decisions to hide how dangerous their platform is because they’re worried about regulation and public pushback,” Edelson said.

In response, OpenAI’s Kwon said: “It is absolutely false to say Chris Lehane was involved with our original referral decision … It’s also completely untrue to say that the people at the center of these challenging decisions do not prioritize safety, or that there are ‘political’ or ‘public relations’ factors at play.”

When the first seven lawsuits were filed against OpenAI in April, the company published a blog post about its “commitment to safety”. Altman also sent a letter to the Tumbler Ridge community apologizing for not notifying Canadian police about what OpenAI knew regarding the shooter’s potential threat.

“While I know words can never be enough, I believe an apology is necessary to recognize the harm and irreversible loss your community has suffered,” Altman wrote.

David Eby, the British Columbia premier, posted the letter to social media with the comment: “The apology is necessary, and yet grossly insufficient for the devastation done to the families of Tumbler Ridge.”

title: UK government does not know what datacentres are being used for, FoI request shows
description: Lack of information raises fears over environmental impact of the AI...
fullText:
Lack of information raises fears over environmental impact of the AI boom

UK politics live – latest updates

The UK government does not know what the country’s datacentres are being used for despite fears over the growing environmental impact of the AI boom.

When asked in a freedom of information (FoI) request who was using the largest sites and what for, the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology said it did “not hold the requested information”. The ministry has since been dissolved.

With hundreds of datacentres awaiting planning permission and 315 queueing to connect to the National Grid, there is growing concern over a lack of transparency and justification for these projects given their environmental impact.

Ministers announced plans in January to allow qualifying datacentres to opt into the Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project scheme. This lets developments bypass local planning committees by securing approval from the government. Campaigners say this “insulates” datacentres from local scrutiny.

Zack Polanski, the Green party leader in England and Wales, said: “The government plans to steamroller over local opposition so private companies can build these facilities – yet they can’t even explain what the benefits are and who is benefiting.”

Datacentres use a huge amount of resources. The Guardian revealed last month that two planned sites will have higher carbon emissions than ExxonMobil in the UK, with concerns raised over how this will fit within the country’s carbon targets.

The government designated datacentres as critical national infrastructure in 2024 and campaigners fear this could mean the water-hungry sites are prioritised over households in times of drought. Water UK, the trade body representing water companies in Britain and Northern Ireland, warned in July that the UK did not have enough water for the datacentre expansion.

Polanski said: “What is more ‘critical’ than people’s access to water? What is more ‘critical’ than our need to transition to a low-energy, low-pollution world so we can put the brakes on climate extremes?”

While there is consensus that datacentres can provide some essential services, there are concerns that developments with a huge environmental impact and local opposition are being prioritised regardless of their use.

Oliver Hayes of Global Action Plan, the environmental charity which submitted the FoI request, said: “It’s highly likely that we’re going to end up seeing datacentres given favourable and preferential treatment when it comes to resources that are actually running chatbots or enabling people to do benign and very wasteful, pointless things.

“At the more serious end, these datacentres could be powering chatbots that enable people to nudify teens without their consent and much worse, frankly.”

With reports that the Scottish government is inching toward a moratorium on new datacentres, there is growing pressure for the UK government to follow suit.

Friends of the Earth is calling for a ban on new sites until environmental safeguards are in place. The campaign group wants the government to publish clear environmental rules for new and existing datacentres, including requirements for 100% additional renewable energy generation for new projects.

Anisah Khan, the campaigns manager at Global Action Plan, said: “When individuals across the country are facing hosepipe bans and essential housebuilding is being delayed because datacentres are gobbling up grid connections, what we need is not more chatbots at any cost.”

The government did not respond to a request for comment over its failure to say what large datacentres were being used for.

A spokesperson said: “A pause on building new datacentres would simply send investment and good jobs abroad, while leaving Britain dependent on other countries for the processing of sensitive health and defence data. Put simply: it would be a disaster for jobs and national security.”

title: Freelancers are getting buried with ‘soulless’ AI slop cleanup: ‘It’s a shame we need to do it’
description:
As more companies turn to AI, they’re hiring freelancers to cleanup its mistakes rather than create original work
Lisa, a freelance graphic designer based in Spain, noticed a shift in her work after the release of ChatGPT in 2022. She went from receiving slow one-off jobs creating logos and packaging to an onslaught of requests asking her to fix versions that were generated by artificial intelligence – from sharpening fuzzy images for printing to turning flawed designs into usable files.
By 2025, Lisa, who asked not to be fully named to avoid solicitations, said 90% of her incoming logo and packaging design requests required cleaning up AI-generated content, work that accounted for 60% to 70% of her annual income. Clients lowballed her;' some AI-generated designs were so flawed that she had to recreate them from scratch and she worried about being complicit in AI-driven copyright infringement.
fullText:
As more companies turn to AI, they’re hiring freelancers to cleanup its mistakes rather than create original work

Lisa, a freelance graphic designer based in Spain, noticed a shift in her work after the release of ChatGPT in 2022. She went from receiving slow one-off jobs creating logos and packaging to an onslaught of requests asking her to fix versions that were generated by artificial intelligence – from sharpening fuzzy images for printing to turning flawed designs into usable files.

“It was just so soulless,” said Lisa, who now focuses on “human-made designs”.

Lisa is part of a growing group of creative freelancers being hired to clean up AI slop, a term used to characterize low-quality, AI-generated output. As businesses use tools like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude to produce marketing copy, illustrations, books and videos, they are hiring creative professionals to humanize AI-generated copy, repair botched images and salvage flawed footage.

The work serves as a stopgap in an increasingly challenging job market, supplementing income for those who freelance full-time or on the side. But clients often underestimate the time and skill involved, expecting cleanup to be quick and cheap when it can require as much work as creating something original, freelancers said. And while the high volume of cleanup gigs can be lucrative, freelancers are divided over the trade-off. Some find it tedious and creatively unfulfilling, while others enjoy the challenge. As AI improves, freelancers question how long the demand will last and where they’ll turn once the jobs dry up.

For now, demand for AI cleanup work is growing.

On Freelancer.com, a contract work platform with more than 88 million users, job listings tagged with phrases such as “correct AI”, “AI hallucination” and “AI error” rose 87% to 10,760 globally between August 2025 and June 2026, according to internal data shared with the Guardian. The jobs were concentrated in graphic design, followed by video editing, proofreading and content writing. Upwork saw AI remediation gigs jump 70% year over year, and Fiverr saw keyword searches for “AI cleanup” services grow more than 20 times between 2023 and 2026, according to data shared with the Guardian.

The specter of AI could spell trouble for the creative freelance labor market. Listings for freelance jobs exposed to automation fell 21% in the eight months after ChatGPT launched and image-creation gigs dropped 17% after AI image generators arrived, according to a 2025 study published in the academic journal Management Science. And those losses have continued, according to a 2026 study.

Meanwhile, more workers are turning to freelance work as companies cut staff and hire less, intensifying competition. The average project on Freelancer.com drew 54 bids in 2025, up 8% from the year before, according to the site’s annual report.

But as companies cut costs, they’re changing the nature of freelance assignments, from requests for creative work to sprucing up AI output. Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com, said the cleanup work is often commissioned by small companies and entrepreneurs using AI to produce a first pass, only to run into problems they don’t have the expertise to solve.

“[AI output] needs a human to turn it into something polished that can actually be used,” he said. The time and money saved on the first draft can be eaten up by the “incredibly time-consuming” work of preparing it for commercial use.

For some freelancers, cleanup is taking up a growing share of their workload and traditional creative projects are becoming harder to find.

Todd Van Linda, a full-time freelance illustrator in Florida, began taking AI cleanup gigs in 2023 as his usual work drawing illustrations, video game art and architectural plans became less steady. The work typically involves filtering out visual noise, improving resolution, and hunting for glitches like an extra toe.

“Money”, Van Linda said of his motivation. “The jobs were there to be done.”

Though some clients expect AI cleanup to cost less than original work, Van Linda won’t lower his rates. When one prospective client offered about $500 to repair 13 to 15 AI-generated illustrations for a children’s book, with the expectation that each should take about 15 minutes, he turned it down. He said projects can take between a few hours of work to days depending on the scope. His rate is $65 an hour and “doesn’t go down from there”, he said.

For Kym Dunbar, a freelance writer and editor based in Australia, AI cleanup now accounts for about 60% of her workload, as writing work like blogs and website copy have dwindled. As a result, Dunbar said her monthly earnings from writing original content have fallen to roughly a third of what she made during the pandemic.

Dunbar stumbled into cleanup work in 2024, when a client asked her to revise an AI-generated article. She quickly learned to spot recurring problems, from repetitive language and awkward paragraph structures to a lack of emotional nuance. Since then, she has worked on about 40 AI-generated nonfiction books, longform articles and technical papers.

“There’s a lot less good projects available for writers and editors these days,” Dunbar said.

But “cleanup” can understate how much work is involved.

Nathan McConnell, a multimedia editor who freelances on top of his full-time job, started editing AI-generated videos in 2023. His work has ranged from removing reflections from AI real estate videos to fixing robotic voiceovers and malformed 3D models. The requests have increased from two or three projects in 2023 to eight to 10 so far this year, he said.

One client brought him roughly 100 AI-generated images of humanoid animals for a tarot deck riddled with extra fingers, two left feet and other mistakes. McConnell spent two to three hours repairing each image in Photoshop, expecting the project to take nearly two weeks to finish. But after making the first 10 cards, he called the project off because of health issues and constant changes requested from his “persnickety” client.

Not everything that lands in McConnell’s inbox can be saved, he said. That could look like videos where the physics feel off, like shadows falling the wrong way, or animations that repurpose another creator’s work without permission.

“I’ve told a client before that it’s ‘too’ slop,” McConnell said. “There’s no way I can fix this.”

While McConnell and Van Linda would rather make original work, not everyone finds fixing AI outputs dispiriting. Dunbar considers it “interesting” and “challenging”, and takes satisfaction in turning a weak draft into polished prose.

What troubles her is that people increasingly see AI not as a tool, but as the “be-all and end-all” of the creative process.

“I just feel it’s a shame we need to do it,” Dunbar said.

It’s unclear whether cleaning up AI-generated slop will remain a viable source of work.

Dunbar isn’t convinced it will. She believes much of the work humanizing AI could dry up within five to 10 years as models improve and allow businesses to generate usable content themselves.

McConnell sees it differently, arguing that AI still needs to be “babysat” to catch mistakes an untrained eye might miss, from logos that violate brand guidelines to objects that appear and disappear in videos. “We need people [to fix] problems that AI is creating,” he said.

But Van Linda is already creating a different path. After he stopped taking AI cleanup gigs late last year, he has seen more clients, some of whom have been dissatisfied with AI, seeking original, hand-drawn work.

“Quite frankly, this kind of thing has gotten extremely distasteful to me,” he said about AI cleanup work.

Though Lisa, the freelance graphic designer, updated her profile to say she no longer works with AI-generated images, she still gets requests to edit them. She occasionally takes cleanup gigs for clients who come to her after getting poor results with AI. But some clients “straight up lie” and pass off the images as original creations.

“They say ‘I don’t use AI,’ but there’s a “[Google] Gemini logo on the bottom,” she said.

But just in case AI makes her job obsolete, she has a plan. Lisa has begun returning to the canvases, watercolors and other physical art she practiced before she pursued a career in graphic design. She predicts that within “another year or two”, AI will be able to do logo and packaging design as well as she can, leaving only “the best of the best” able to make a living.

“I don’t know if I’m good enough to survive the digital stuff,” she said.

title: Tim Cook handed $47m package for new role as executive chair of Apple
description: Pay and shares deal nearly matches $58m award to John Ternus, his successor as CEO at the $4.7tn tech...
fullText:
Pay and shares deal nearly matches $58m award to John Ternus, his successor as CEO at the $4.7tn tech company

Tim Cook has received a $47m (£35m) pay deal as Apple’s executive chair, a remuneration package that nears the level set for his successor as chief executive.

Cook, who handed over to John Ternus on Tuesday, will be paid a base salary of $2m and $45m worth of shares. Half of the share award will be based on performance targets being met, while the remaining half will be paid out over four years.

Ternus will receive a base salary of $3m and a $55m share award, with the latter more weighted to performance.

Cook’s total compensation as chief executive for 2025 exceeded $74m. Cook, who owns more than 3m shares in Apple, has been placed in the multi-billionaire category by Forbes, which estimates his wealth at $3bn.

His predecessor, the Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, was paid a symbolic $1 a year but was worth $7bn when he died, including a sizeable shareholding in Disney he acquired after selling the Pixar animation studio to the entertainment conglomerate.

Cook took over from Jobs in 2011 having impressed as an operations specialist. The stock has risen 2,200% since he took charge, with Apple now valued at about $4.7tn – compared with about $350bn when he became chief executive.

He built the tech company’s sophisticated supply chain and is succeeded by a 51-year-old engineer and longstanding Apple employee, who built products as senior vice-president of hardware engineering.

Ternus’s role meant he ran the engineering teams behind Apple’s entire product lineup, including the iPhones that generate most of the company’s revenue. Analysts are not only anticipating new products but also further progress on integrating AI into Apple hardware.

Ternus’s first big public moment at Apple will be at its annual iPhone event on 9 September, where a foldable handset is expected to be revealed. New iterations of the Apple Watch and AirPods are also anticipated, although Bloomberg reported last week that AirPods with cameras – another big product rumour – “aren’t launching anytime soon”.

Cook’s new mandate includes engaging with policymakers around the world and will involve maintaining the company’s relationship with Donald Trump, as well as overseeing the company’s diplomatic ties with China – a key production hub. In a final memo to employees on Monday, he focused on Apple’s products.

“I will miss leading you and being with you for every step, even as I take enormous comfort in handing the helm to someone as brilliant and wonderful and capable as John,” he said. “Few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does.”

Trump Can’t Stop the Populist Uprising Against Data Centers
description: Chris...
fullText:
The grassroots revolt against AI oligarchs is reviving a more than a century-old fight against robber barons and their attempts to seize land, water, and political power.

There’s a hulking irony taking shape across the landscape of the 2026 midterms: After a decade of pundits bloviating about the menace of populism in our times, the material conditions that gave rise to American populism have upended the political consensus. In the tirelessly mythologized heartland said to harbor the recondite attitudes and mindset of MAGA-era populism, disenchanted citizens are staging an uprising over the plutocratic seizure of land and resources engineered by a new generation of robber barons. As AI data centers suck up water, land, and political capital—while spewing gas-generated carbon emissions at dangerous new levels—ordinary Americans in the country’s post-industrial interior are in open revolt. The backlash against data centers is now so potent that candidates in both major parties are scrambling to no longer be identified with the tech lords dedicated to disfiguring the country.

The opposition to data centers in red states has grown so strident that President Donald Trump intervened on behalf of his benefactors in the AI industry. In a Truth Social post on Monday, Trump sought to browbeat his followers into submission, claiming the data centers poised to set up Borg-like in their midst will serve both their own economic self-interest and the dictates of national security. The MAGA nation should “let Data Reign,” Trump pronounced—unless, that is, its strongholds would prefer to be “backwards and poor.” “If we kill the Golden Goose,” Trump continued, showing that his mastery of fairy tales is equivalent to his prowess with capitalization, “you will have only yourselves to blame.” Perhaps sensing that any appeal to the alleged equal distribution of the wealth arising from the biggest and most oligarch-friendly investment bubble in human history would fall flat, the president tried to scold the MAGA faithful into recognizing their patriotic duty: “China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement. Actually, they can’t believe it is happening!”

It didn’t go over well. “This statement is insane,” went one typical reply on the traditionally Trump-idolizing platform. “I’m already on water restriction.” Another plaint got more personal: “You’re an idiot. You’ll be making money I expect. Meanwhile our lives get shittier with no water, more noise.” One of the more measured responses accurately summed up Trump’s outburst as “horrendous messaging.”

Behind such unrest in the house of MAGA is a larger truth: Nobody wants a data center anywhere near them. A recent Heatmap News poll drives home how dramatically public opinion has shifted on the issue: A year ago, data centers won 43 percent net support and clocked 42 percent opposition. Now, in that same poll, 75 percent of respondents oppose the construction of data centers near them, and just 15 percent support them—a swing of 61 percent. Sorting through this seismic turnaround, Ryan Cooper of The American Prospect surmises that it’s part of a broader repudiation of the arrogant impunity of the tech-industry power elite:

The AI rollout has been the ne plus ultra of Silicon Valley arrogance. A handful of billionaires—whose steadily more incomprehensible podcast appearances indicate participation in some truly unhinged group chats, or consumption of heavy-duty chemicals, or membership in literal, no-joke cults, or all three—declaimed that AI was going to revolutionize all human society, take everyone’s job, and/or maybe wipe out the human race. Therefore they needed to spend trillions and trillions of dollars building AI data centers everywhere, as fast as possible. When the tech barons blearily realized that this wasn’t the best sales pitch, and pivoted to ads about how AI had dull business applications, the damage was already done.

All true enough—yet the other, more immediate cause of the data-center revolt has to do with basic principles of communal self-protection: No one wants the austerity represented by water rationing, spikes in electrical bills, and general resource plunder to wipe out the quality of life in the places where you live and work. And this is where the precedent of 19th-century Populism–the real, capital-P article—becomes useful. When you squint a bit at the data-center uprising, its economic message is of a piece with the Populists’ crusade to rein in the brutal takeover of the American countryside by the twinned forces of the railroad and oil industries. The great Populist apostle of reform politics, Henry Demarest Lloyd, laid out the case against the oil and rail monopolies in an 1881 muckraking report for The Atlantic Monthly titled—yes—Story of a Great Monopoly. As he chronicled how railroads controlled farmers’ access to crucial markets—and how, in concert with the new Standard Oil empire, colluded to fix prices and drive up costs for farms already steeped in debt—he described a new first-order threat to the basic conditions of self-government in America. As long as the republic was in the grip of the railroad monopoly, most of its fundamental operations were throttled into oligarchic submission:

It is the railroads that have bred the millionaires who are now buying newspapers, and getting up corners in wheat, corn, and cotton, and are making railroad consolidations that stretch across the continent. By the same tactics that the railroads have used to build up the Standard [Oil Company], they can give other combinations of capitalists the control of the wheat, lumber, cotton, or any other product of the United States. . . . In less than the ordinary span of a life-time, our railroads have brought upon us the worst labor disturbances, the greatest of monopolies, and the most formidable combination of money and brains that ever overshadowed a state. . . . The common people, the nation, must take them in hand. The people can be successful only when they are right. When monopolies succeed, the people fail; when a rich criminal escapes justice, the people are punished; when a legislature is bribed, the people are cheated.

It’s striking to note how fully Lloyd’s indictment of the railroad monopoly maps on to today’s revolt against the data centers. Now, as then, legislatures are the plaything of the monopolists remaking the country into their own image—Republican candidates for Congress desperately want to memory-hole this data point, but the entire GOP majority in the House, minus just five dissenters, voted for a provision in Trump’s signature 2025 spending bill that would have forbidden states and localities from regulating the AI industry or its data-center infrastructure for a decade. That’s very much equivalent to the habit of Gilded Age railroad monarchs essentially purchasing compliant state legislatures to do their bidding.

Then there are the resource squeezes. Just as today’s AI lords are making water scarce and electricity more expensive, railroads extended preferential rates to John D. Rockefeller’s Standard Oil operations while driving other smaller market players out of business and erecting the resource cartels that Lloyd and other muckrakers tirelessly chronicled.

The data-center uprising also echoes the Populist campaign against monopoly in its cross-partisan appeal. During the first Gilded Age, the major parties were enmeshed in a plutocratic consensus not unlike the one that’s controlled our own politics during the past generation, with apologists for regressive financial policies such as the gold standard and the readily gamed tariff system occupying key leadership positions in both parties. The AI oligarchy has accordingly hard-wired much of the leadership faction across the partisan aisle to do its bidding; House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries opposes a moratorium on data-center construction, just like his counterpart, House Speaker Mike Johnson, does. Establishment Democrats felt like they’d dodged a bullet when Wisconsin’s socialist candidate for governor Francesca Hong lost to former Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley—only to see Crowley’s general-election campaign thrown back on its heels by his support for data centers. Of course, the Populists sought to break the stranglehold of plutocratic governance by founding their own independent party, which was then a more viable strategy for reform politics; it’s an indictment of our duopolistic status quo that neither party, as a principled matter of political economy, can afford to divorce itself from today’s tech oligarchy.

That, in turn, underlines the key difference between the anti-monopolists of the Gilded Age and the scourges of the tech oligarchy combating the far-reaching zoning putsches behind the planned construction of more than 2,000 new data centers: They had a clear policy objective, which was to advance the public ownership of the railroads and other utilities. “We believe the time has come when the railroad corporations will either own the people or the people must own the railroads,” the Populists declared in their 1892 Omaha Platform. No political leader today has advanced a similar case for taking over the predatory and resource-hoarding tech monopoly, but ideas along these lines might take hold in a cross-party bid to reclaim the basic conditions of self-determination in our communities. And they might have gained far more serious traction by now if we’d been in the throes of an actual Populist insurgency over the past decade, as opposed to the phony reality-television one that our pundit class ritually deplores.

title: Pub's 'beloved' manager stabbed to death in Germany
description: Rebecca Bullock, 31, was attacked at Rosenheim station on Sunday.
fullText:
A pub has paid tribute to its "beloved" manager after she was stabbed to death in Germany.

Rebecca Bullock, 31, was attacked at Rosenheim station shortly before 01:00 local time (00:00 BST) on Sunday. She was taken to hospital but later died.

Bavarian Police said a 27-year-old German man, of no fixed address, was arrested at the scene and later detained in a psychiatric hospital on suspicion of murder.

The White Swan, in Whitchurch, Buckinghamshire, said: "We are so deeply sorry to say that our beloved Becca passed away over the weekend whilst away on holiday."

"Becca was much-loved by all of the team at the White Swan and our amazing locals," its Facebook post read.

The pub closed from Monday after what it described as a "tough few days", but its landlords said it would reopen from 15:00.

They said: "We know this is what Becca would have wanted."

A Foreign Office spokesperson told the BBC: "We are supporting the family of a British woman who died in Germany [and] are in touch with the local authorities."

The 31-year-old ran the London Marathon in 2022 in aid of the Milton Keynes-based Spinal Injuries Association, having undergone three spinal operations herself.

She was also a member of Thame Runners in Oxfordshire, which said it was "deeply saddened" by her death.

In July, she and her clubmates were part of the winning women's team at the Waddesdon 5k in Buckinghamshire.

"She will be remembered with great affection by the many members who knew her, ran alongside her and shared in her love of running," the club said.

Tributes were also paid by the joint masters of the "Bicester Hunt with Whaddon Chase", where she was a secretary.

They said: "Becca was a vital and much-loved part of our hunt, both as a dedicated secretary and as a dear friend to so many.

"Her loss is being felt deeply across our entire community, of which she was such an integral part. We extend our heartfelt sympathies to her family and friends at this incredibly difficult time."

title: Warsh's Jackson Hole encore may put Trump's inflation record under a microscope
description: After opening the door to higher interest rates last week, U.S.
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Sept 2 (Reuters) - After opening the door to higher interest rates last week, U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh has to decide how to follow through with actions the public and investors will see as both consistent with his own words and independent of President Donald Trump's wishes.

How might September rate decisions affect midterm elections?

What inflation data will influence Fed's September meeting?

What did Fed Chairman Warsh signal about interest rates?

What challenges does Warsh face regarding Fed credibility?

Failing those tests could be a blow to the new Fed chief's credibility. Passing them may mean a rate hike later this month, a powerful signal from the U.S. central bank's policy committee — less than two ‌months before key congressional elections — that Trump has failed to contain inflation and will not get the Fed's help in lowering borrowing costs on the rising national debt.

In a speech to the Kansas City Fed's annual Jackson Hole conference in Wyoming on Friday, Warsh went further ‌than many observers expected in agreeing that higher rates may be needed to curb inflation that is stuck above the central bank's 2% target.

He will face problems, however, "if the data for August do not line up well with the decision the committee makes in September," said Robert Tetlow, a former senior policy adviser at the Fed. "Having campaigned so transparently for the job makes the ​scrutiny he is facing that much more intense."

Trump has said he believes Warsh, appointed by the president to lead the central bank, wants to cut rates but is prevented by others at the Fed whom the president sees as "hostile" and "political." Trump on Monday repeated that the U.S. should have "the lowest interest rates anywhere in the world," despite $40 trillion in outstanding government debt and high annual deficits, but said Warsh would "do what he has to" and still had his respect.

Now that the Fed chief has laid down a rate-hike marker of his own, "the onus is on Warsh to deliver. ... Otherwise, he risks undermining some of the credibility he gained," Aditya Bhave and Shruti Mishra, U.S. economists at Bank of America, wrote following the Jackson Hole speech.

Fed policymakers will meet on September 15-16. Investors now see a roughly two-to-one chance the central bank will approve a quarter-percentage-point hike in the overnight policy rate, which has been held in the 3.50%-3.75% range since December. Odds of a hike later this ‌month jumped after Warsh's remarks at Jackson Hole, and again on Monday following renewed U.S. strikes on Iran ⁠and another rise in the interest rate investors demand to hold long-term U.S. government debt.

Three of the Fed's 12 voting policymakers were ready to raise rates at the July 28-29 meeting and dissented against the decision to leave them unchanged.

title: Graduates of a small West Coast college are earning more than Harvard and Stanford alums. Here's why.
description: Samuel Merritt University, a small college in the Bay Area, has some of America's highest-earning graduates — thanks to its focus and location.
fullText:
Business Insider ranked the top colleges for graduate pay across the US.

The Education Department's College Scorecard tracks median earnings four years after graduation.

Samuel Merritt University, a small California nursing school, ranked third in US graduate earnings.

Some of the highest-earning college graduates in the US may not have a Harvard degree hanging on the wall.

In a recent Business Insider ranking of US colleges with the highest-earning graduates, a small Bay Area school focused on health sciences outperformed Stanford and Harvard, as well as the rest of the Ivy League schools.

Meet Samuel Merritt University, a nursing and health-focused private nonprofit university in Oakland, California, with fewer than 1,000 undergraduate students.

Graduates from the university have a median income of $148,182 four years after graduation, ranking third in the country for graduate pay according to the US Department of Education's College Scorecard, which measures the yearly post-graduation earnings of students who received federal aid such as student loans or work-study grants.

Samuel Merritt University doesn't offer on-campus housing and instead partners with local properties to provide discounted housing rates for students. It also has a food pantry that students can access.

While the student experience is different from that at larger colleges, students praise the sense of community and diversity the school offers.

"My peers are not only dedicated to their own growth but also collaborative and supportive, which has created an environment where I feel encouraged and motivated to do my best," a senior student wrote on Niche.

Students in the school's primary nursing bachelor's program take on an average of $20,000 in federal student loan debt and have post-graduation earnings comparable to those of graduates with a liberal arts and sciences degree from MIT, which ranked first in the nation for graduate pay across all disciplines.

Since Samuel Merritt University has a strong focus on nursing and other related healthcare professions, it helps boost its earnings ranking.

According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, registered nurses earned an average of $101,420 nationwide in 2025. In California, the average was $150,280, the highest of any US state.

Beyond the school's focus on healthcare, its prime location in the Bay Area contributes to its graduates' high earnings.

With some of the highest costs of living in the nation, the Bay Area also has some of the highest incomes in the US.

In the San Francisco metro area, households have a median annual income of $135,590, according to the Census Bureau's 2024 American Community Survey. The metro area has the highest median household income among the 25 most populous US metro areas.

Samuel Merritt's health sciences focus, and its graduates' strong presence in California's high-wage healthcare market, likely help explain why its federally aided graduates report higher median earnings than those from some Ivy League schools.
