title: Sri Lanka stripped of hosting Women's Champions Trophy
description: The International Cricket Council moves the inaugural edition of next year's Women's Champions Trophy from Sri Lanka to India.
fullText:
Next year's inaugural Women's Champions Trophy has been moved from Sri Lanka to India by the International Cricket Council.

Sri Lanka had been due to stage the six-team event but have been stripped of the hosting rights because of ongoing issues with its national board and government interference.

A statement from the ICC said Sri Lanka Cricket is continuing "to make the requisite reforms" which were outlined at the global governing body's annual conference in July.

Bangladesh and South Africa were also interested in staging the tournament but the ICC board ratified India as replacement hosts for the event, with matches to be held in Mumbai and Vadodara.

Unlike the men's Champions Trophy, which is a 50-over-a-side competition, the women's event will be a T20 tournament.

It will be played on a round-robin basis with the top two sides progressing to the final.

Australia, England, India, New Zealand, South Africa and Sri Lanka are the six teams who will take part, having been the highest-ranked sides at the qualification cut-off date of 6 July.

title: 'Zero excuses' - Wardley out to avenge Dubois loss
description: Fabio Wardley says there are "zero excuses" heading into his highly anticipated rematch with WBO heavyweight champion Daniel Dubois on 17 October.
fullText:
Fabio Wardley says there are "zero excuses" heading into his highly anticipated rematch with WBO heavyweight champion Daniel Dubois on 17 October as he looks to write a new chapter in his story.

Wardley, 31, dropped fellow Briton Dubois twice when they fought in May but was stopped in round 11 and lost his world title.

The Ipswich fighter immediately triggered his rematch clause and will look to avenge the only defeat of his career at London's O2 Arena.

"I have zero excuses for the loss on the night and zero excuses going into the rematch," Wardley said at Wednesday's launch news conference.

"It's just another chapter in the story that is my career.

"By no means did I expect to get through boxing unscathed - not many do. Even Daniel has proven you can take a loss and come back, he's a two-time heavyweight champion."

Dubois was coming off the third defeat of his 26-fight career when he showed courage to twice get off the canvas to overcome Wardley.

The 28-year-old, who also held the IBF title in 2024, vowed to seize his opportunity to build momentum with another victory as he looks to unify in 2027.

"I was coming off a defeat so I was a bit nervous. It's a fresh start for me," said Dubois.

"I want to be the last man standing and be up there with the greats."

October's rematch was announced on Saturday at the O2 Arena when Dubois and Wardley faced off in the ring moments before Moses Itauma's defeat by Filip Hrgovic for the IBF heavyweight title.

Dubois and Wardley both said on Wednesday that they had a new-found respect for each other after going through a gruelling 11 rounds earlier in the year.

But there was a tense moment when they faced off at the news conference, with Wardley asking "can we be cool?" before Dubois responded "after the fight, man".

A confused-looking Wardley said: "Do you not like me? I thought after the fight we were all right?"

There were several awkward moments in the build-up to their first bout, with Dubois refusing Wardley's fist bump, and there was a similar situation when they crossed paths backstage before their latest media engagement.

Reflecting on their first meeting, Wardley said he has learned from his mistakes and will ensure they are corrected.

"I lost a bit of, not to say the old me, but I felt a bit too comfortable with the really early knockdown followed by another in the third. I relaxed into the fight thinking I've done it twice and I can get him out of there," Wardley said.

"I think I was a victim of my own success and got trigger happy. I was carried away with launching my right hand and trying to finish it.

"I was too relaxed, comfortable and laid back in certain scenarios."

Dubois kept his answers short, insisting he is not looking beyond Wardley, but Queensberry chief Frank Warren painted a picture of how bright the future might look for the winner.

Queensberry have built a strong stable of heavyweights over recent years and have three of the four world champions in their ranks.

Alongside WBO champion Dubois, Warren has WBC champion Agit Kabayel and newly crowned IBF title-holder Filip Hrgovic.

Warren's intention is to keep those belts in-house and he plans to ensure they are all active in 2027.

"We'll be working hard to make the unifications - that's our plan," Warren said.

"Next year it's about getting them all together. We're doing something that even Don King didn't do. They are fighting regularly in big fights."

title: Hampshire make Kuggeleijn U-turn after criticism
description: Hampshire decide that New Zealand all-rounder Scott Kuggeleijn will not represent the club having "listened to feedback from staff and supporters".
fullText:
Hampshire have decided that New Zealand all-rounder Scott Kuggeleijn will not represent the club having "listened to feedback from staff and supporters".

On Tuesday the Rose and Crown named him in their squad for a County Championship match against Warwickshire without announcing his signing on their social channels.

The signing received criticism on social media and less than an hour before the start of play on Wednesday the county said that Kuggeleijn would not play any role in their final four games.

Kuggeleijn, 34, faced a rape charge in 2015 and after a re-trial due to a hung jury he was acquitted in 2017.

It is understood that the player was in attendance at Utilita Bowl for the first day of the game on Wednesday.

"Having reflected and listened to feedback from staff and supporters Hampshire Cricket can confirm that Scott Kuggeleijn will not represent the club," the county said in a statement. , external

"We value the passion of our fanbase and thank everyone who took the time to share their views.

"Our focus now turns to supporting the team through the final four County Championship fixtures of the season.

"We encourage everyone to unite behind the team as we enter a crucial stage of the campaign."

Seam bowler Kuggeleijn has spent 12 years playing for Northern Districts in his home country.

He has also played three Test matches for the Black Caps as well as two one-day internationals and 18 T20s.

Hampshire currently sit bottom of Division One in the County Championships on 86 points, 16 points below Leicestershire above them.

The Rose and Crown have only won twice with the red ball this year, losing on five occasions and drawing three.

title: Man Utd and their calculated left-back gamble
description: Despite a widespread expectation they would sign a left-back this summer, Manchester United decided against - what does it mean?
fullText:
As 23:00 BST ticked by on 1 September and the suspicion became reality, many Manchester United fans thought the same thing – what about a left-back?

Since the 2025-26 season ended, and United's summer transfer strategy started to be debated, it seemed obvious the club would move to address a perceived weakness in Michael Carrick's squad.

Luke Shaw is their only senior orthodox left-back. He started all 38 Premier League games last season, which given his previous injury record was phenomenal.

But as back-up Tyrell Malacia had unsurprisingly been allowed to leave when his contract expired at the end of June, and it is widely accepted 31-year-old Shaw will not be able to play repeatedly in a new campaign that could stretch beyond 60 games, a reinforcement was expected.

Various targets were identified, including Newcastle's Lewis Hall, Barcelona's Alejandro Balde and Racing Santander's Jorge Salinas. Finally, it came down to an attempt to get Rayan Ait-Nouri to cross the great Manchester divide by joining on loan, but City said no.

For that move to have progressed, United would have had to include an obligation to buy at a later date, but have instead chosen to bide their time for their first-choice targets.

Now the deadline has passed and, at least until the winter window opens in January, United and Carrick must stand or fall by what has to be viewed as a calculated gamble.

Man Utd fail in attempt to sign Ait-Nouri from Man City

Firstly, it must be acknowledged Manchester United really like Lewis Hall.

Had they been able to do a deal with Newcastle for him, they would have done.

However, raided by Premier League rivals for their star men this summer, it became obvious in discussions around the highly-rated 22-year-old if Newcastle were to be persuaded to strike a deal, the transfer fee would be huge.

Manchester United's summer transfer budget was finite.

Faced with the reality of the situation, they opted to maintain their focus on the 'priority' midfield area and eventually committed £70m to bring in Carlos Baleba from Brighton.

Hall, it was concluded, is someone they are prepared to wait until next summer for.

United would have been prepared to take Balde on loan. Barcelona would only sell him. Salinas had a relatively low release clause, but Atletico Madrid were favourites to sign him. By the time they moved on to Argentina defender Nicolas Tagliafico, who they missed out on anyway, United had moved on themselves.

Their decision to belatedly act on an initial approach made by an agent around Ait-Nouri was an admission they are not totally certain of the path they have chosen.

Effectively that is Shaw as first-choice left-back, with Noussair Mazraoui as back-up, in a position he admittedly plays in for Morocco, supported by Diogo Dalot, who has switched flanks before, and Harry Amass.

The Amass case is a strange one. A natural left-back in United's academy, who did well in a loan spell at Sheffield Wednesday last season, then got injured straight after switching to Norwich in the winter window, Amass, 19, impressed many observers with his performances during pre-season, when he shadowed Shaw.

Yet, for some reason, United were willing to let him leave.

In the summer of 2024, then manager Erik ten Hag opted not to pick the teenager in his squad for the Community Shield, even though Amass had given a creditable account of himself up against Mo Salah in a pre-season game in the United States just a week earlier.

Ten Hag felt, physically, Amass was not at the level required. In theory, the two years that have elapsed since then should have made the defender bigger and stronger.

There have been multiple expressions of interest in Amass. Even heading into deadline day, his omission from United's Premier League 2 game against Leicester on Monday reinforced a widespread belief he would leave, probably on loan.

But that has not happened and it is not clear what his role will be within the senior squad.

The willingness to view Mazraoui as a left-back option was helped by the performances of Leny Yoro in pre-season.

Signed from Lille for £52m in 2024 as a central defender, Carrick used Yoro mainly as a right-back this summer.

Against Ipswich on Sunday, that was the slot Yoro was introduced into as a replacement for Dalot, at the same time as Mazraoui was coming on for Shaw.

At just 20, Yoro has plenty to learn about the right-back role. However, he has pace, is strong and is good on the ball. United supporters only have to look at how Josko Gvardiol has adapted to the full-back role at Manchester City after signing as a central defender to realise switching positions can have a positive outcome.

That is the calculated risk United have taken.

What they absolutely did not want to do, having taken a hardline stance all summer on the fees they were willing to pay, and a refusal to spend more than they thought a player was worth, was end up making a signing like Alex Telles, or Matteo Darmian, or Sergio Reguilon, who all arrived in recent years but were evidently short of the standard required.

It makes sense. It is probably the right call.

But that is a view taken away from the emotion of matches and the rollercoaster of results. And the reality is they will be the deciding factor in whether it was a good decision or not.

title: Who are the free agents after transfer deadline day?
description: BBC Sport takes a look at the players still without a club after the 2026 summer transfer window shut.
fullText:
The summer transfer window is closed but there are still a host of talented players without a club and therefore available to sign for free.

BBC Sport takes a look at some of the biggest stars who are currently out of contract and up for grabs.

Paul Pogba, 33 (Last club: Monaco)

Former Manchester United midfielder Pogba has played very little football since his 18 month doping ban ended in March 2025. The Frenchman made just six appearances for Monaco after joining them last summer and, after a series of injuries, the French club terminated his contract last month - one year before it was due to end.

Karim Benzema, 38 (Last club: Al Hilal)

French striker Benzema has been plying his trade in Saudi Arabia since leaving Real Madrid in 2023, spending three years with Al Ittihad. But just six months after joining Al-Hilal the Ballon d'Or winner has terminated his contract. The arrival of attacking trio Crysencio Summerville, Ollie Watkins and Gabriel Martinelli has perhaps pushed Benzema out and, despite already making three appearances for Al-Hilal this season, his contract was terminated on 31 August.

Riyad Mahrez, 35 (Last club: Al Ahli)

Another player to have had their contract terminated in the Saudi Pro League is five-time Premier League winner Mahrez. The Algeria winger joined Al Ahli from Manchester City in 2023, scoring 37 goals in 122 appearances in all competitions. Reports suggest he will stay in the Saudi league and is close to joining Al-Shabab.

Raheem Sterling, 31 (Last club: Feyenoord)

Sterling was released by Feyenoord after just three months and eight games and is set to appear in court next month to face charges of dangerous driving after crashing his car into motorway barriers in May. Sources told BBC Sport the former Manchester City, Liverpool and Chelsea winger had faced "an extremely tough couple of years".

Philippe Coutinho, 34 (Last club: Vasco da Gama)

Former Liverpool and Barcelona midfielder Coutinho left his boyhood club Vasco de Gama in February, saying he was "tired mentally". The Brazilian has not officially announced his retirement and has previously been linked with a move to the MLS.

Jadon Sancho, 26 (Last club: Manchester United)

It has been a turbulent few years for Sancho since joining United from Borussia Dortmund for £73m in 2021 and he has spent the last two and-a-half years playing elsewhere on loan, most recently at Aston Villa following a lacklustre period at Chelsea. Sancho made just 30 Premier League appearances for United but has reportedly agreed a move to Brazilian club Palmeiras.

Dani Carvajal, 34 (Last club: Real Madrid)

Widely regarded as one of the best right-backs of his generation, Carvajal has been a free agent since his contract with Real Madrid ended in June. Carvajal made 451 appearances across all competitions for Real in 13 years and has not been linked with a new club. He has reportedly been training at the Spanish Football Federation's facilities over the summer with compatriot and fellow free agent Joselu.

Jamie Vardy, 39 (Last club: Cremonese)

Vardy spent last season with Cremonese after 13 years with Leicester City but relegation to Serie B prompted the Italian side to let the striker go. He has been heavily linked with a move back to the English Football League with Wrexham, Sheffield Wednesday and West Ham all reportedly interested.

David Alaba, 34 (Last club: Real Madrid)

Experienced full-back Alaba left Real Madrid in May after five years with the club and, for a spell this summer, Manchester United were the bookies' favourite to sign the Austrian. The former Bayern Munich star has had a storied club career that has yielded 12 league titles and four Champions Leagues. Despite speculation of interest from a number of clubs as his Real contract came to an end, so far, Alaba has not signed for anyone.

Sergio Ramos, 40 (Last club: Monterrey)

Legendary Spanish defender Ramos has been without a club since December 2025 after leaving Mexican side Monterrey. Although aged 40, he has not announced his retirement while some reports suggest he still feels fit enough to compete at a high level. Earlier this year he spearheaded a consortium who attempted to acquire a controlling stake in his former club Sevilla but the bid failed.

title: How Everton's deadline day debacle leaves owners facing fan mutiny
description: Everton's transfer deadline day debacle over Folarin Balogun leaves owners The Friedkin facing fan mutiny, says chief football writer Phil McNulty.
fullText:
Everton's shambolic end to the transfer window has resulted in open revolt from supporters that places fierce scrutiny on owners The Friedkin Group and chief executive Angus Kinnear.

The last straw for fans already infuriated by the controversial proposed sale of home-grown youngster Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest - the deal was eventually blocked by Everton's board in the face of the toxic reaction from the fanbase - was the bungled final day before the window closed.

Folarin Balogun's proposed £40m move from AS Monaco descended into high farce in the early hours of Wednesday morning after the original deal was renegotiated when issues arose with his medical, ending with the United States striker deciding to walk away from Everton's Finch Farm training base without signing.

And all after Balogun, 25, and both clubs had signed the deal sheet allowing the move to be completed after Tuesday's 23.00 BST transfer deadline.

Everton had scheduled an 8am flight to bring Balogun to Merseyside, but he was unable to arrive until later in the day. Everton were also frustrated at a delay in receiving documents related to the deal from Monaco.

When the problem with his medical cropped up, it prompted Everton to pursue a loan deal for Manchester United's Joshua Zirkzee, who was happy to sign but was not allowed to leave Old Trafford. A move was also made for Aston Villa's Tammy Abraham but did not progress as the striker wished to remain at Villa Park.

After failing to sign an alternative, a deal was eventually agreed with Monaco, minutes before the deadline, which would have resulted in a smaller up-front payment and a series of triggered payments based on how he progressed. The player's personal terms were unchanged.

It was only then that the former Arsenal striker had his change of heart, leaving Finch Farm with Monaco sporting director Thiago Scuro telling journalists at a news conference on Wednesday that Balogun was "not comfortable" with how Everton treated him during his medical.

Everton believe they supported Balogun throughout the process, while being open about the issues identified. The club also made clear to the player they would work with Monaco to explore a solution that could still enable the transfer to be completed.

To make matters worse, and to shed an even more unflattering light on the club's strategy and operation, it all came hours after Everton had sanctioned striker Beto's £15.5m move to Fiorentina.

Events unfolded as Everton's most creative player Iliman Ndiaye was completing his £65m move to Manchester City.

Everton could point to the fact Balogun took a personal decision they could not reverse, but the bigger question is why they took until the final day of the window to address glaring long-term issues?

Kinnear, in what must now be looked upon as an ill-fated recent interview with BBC Radio Merseyside, announced Everton's squad was "in a good place", adding: "The challenge is we want to get the absolute best player we can in their position. Our metric is that by the close of the transfer window we have achieved that."

He also relayed the views of Everton's American owners that they regarded missing out on Europe last season as "failure". It was an announcement manager David Moyes admitted came as a "surprise".

After the events of recent days, the word "failure" is being applied to the owners and chief executive, not Moyes. And there will be no hiding place for TFG and Kinnear should things now go wrong.

The "good place" Kinnear spoke about has eventually amounted to leaving Moyes with just one striker in the raw Thierno Barry and only 18 senior, outfield players, a parlous state of affairs for the 63-year-old Scot, who has at times found it hard to disguise his dissatisfaction with the extent of the summer's transfer business.

Everton may have re-signed Jack Grealish on loan, and finally solved a right-back problem stretching back years by signing Ashley Maitland-Niles from Lyon for £3m, but the over-riding verdict on the club's transfer window has to be one of huge embarrassment for TFG and Kinnear.

Even the search for a right-back, a problem from last summer and further back, was not smooth, with Maitland-Niles being officially announced shortly after midnight after a £9.4m deal for Fulham's Kenny Tete was shelved when the Cottagers could not find a suitable replacement.

As well as only one striker in Barry, Everton's squad now has just one recognised right-back in Maitland-Niles and one left-back in Vitaliy Mykolenko after youngster Adam Aznou was allowed to join Malaga on loan.

The last few days have seen one major PR catastrophe narrowly avoided by pulling out of the sale of 19-year-old Armstrong, arguably Everton's most promising academy product since Wayne Rooney, only to walk straight into another, highly damaging one.

After the Carabao Cup second-round win at Preston North End, Moyes said: "I still think we have got a lot of work to do. We need more players. Our squad is not big enough and we need to get more quality in some areas if we can do."

Moyes' thoughts will be worth much more than a penny, should he choose to air them publicly, while fans' groups have wasted no time in expressing their undisguised anger, with a petition even set up calling for Kinnear's resignation.

"The Everton Fans' Forum" issued a lengthy statement featuring widescale criticism of the club, saying the Toffees' squad had been left "dangerously short" in key areas.

It added: "The conclusion of this summer's transfer window leaves Everton supporters with serious questions about the club's planning, recruitment and decision-making.

"This is not about demanding that Everton spend recklessly. Supporters understand the financial restrictions the club operates under. We are not demanding marquee signings simply for the sake of it.

"We are demanding competence, preparation and accountability."

And the influential group "The 1878s", volunteers who have created huge flags, banners and tifos to enhance the atmosphere at Everton's new Hill Dickinson Stadium, and whose efforts were described as "unbelievable" by Moyes, has responded to deadline day in similar vein.

In a statement it said it is "standing down for the foreseeable future" in protest, saying: "Like the rest of our fanbase, we are utterly disappointed and disgusted with how this transfer window has gone, especially the end of it.

"Also for fans asking, just to reiterate - when we design flags, there are rules and regulations that we have to adhere to regarding the wording on our flags during displays, we are not allowed derogatory or offensive wording or images.

"If we were able to get a load of flags in the ground to show our feelings of discontent, disappointment and anger over this whole situation, believe us, we would, but this is something that simply wouldn't be allowed."

As well as the last-day signings of Grealish and Maitland-Niles, Everton did make other acquisitions during the window, bringing in PFA Championship Player of the Year Hayden Hackney from Middlesbrough.

Christian Norgaard was signed from Arsenal - although the 32-year-old Dane is currently injured with no comeback date - as a replacement for departed veteran Idrissa Gueye.

Deals for young German Merlin Rohl and England Under-21 winger Tyrique George, on loan last season, were confirmed. Brennan Johnson arrived from Crystal Palace in a straight swap with Dwight McNeil.

All this, however, has been overshadowed by a transfer deadline day that ended as nothing short of a debacle. In reality, they have ended this transfer markedly weaker than when they started it.

Everton are yet to issue any public statement on the events that have led to such damning criticism, fan rebellion and a loss of credibility for owners TFG - but there are many fences to be mended.

If that can be done successfully remains to be seen.

title: Jalen Brunson Shares How He is a ‘Star Role Player’ After Accepting Limited Responsibilities With Mavs
description: There are a number of success stories in the NBA, and Jalen Brunson is arguably one of the most relatable. The New York Knicks star led the team to a championship after a 23-year drought. While all five members of the starting lineup played like there was no tomorrow, stepping up as heroes in each [...]
fullText:
There are a number of success stories in the NBA, and Jalen Brunson is arguably one of the most relatable.

The New York Knicks star led the team to a championship after a 23-year drought. While all five members of the starting lineup played like there was no tomorrow, stepping up as heroes in each of their four wins in the final dance, Brunson played the biggest role.

He was the smallest player on the court, something critic think is his ultimate disadvantage. Still his heart was big enough to make 7-foot-4 Victor Wembanyama tremble. It was a scenario that seemed impossible for him just four years ago.

Brunson came to the league in 2018 after a successful college career with the Villanova Wildcats. The Dallas Mavericks drafted him 33rd overall, and there weren't many expectations surrounding him, especially because the Mavs selected future superstar Luka Doncic in the same draft.

He accepted that role, but how he embraced it is what made the difference.

In an interview with the Road Trippin' show, the 2026 Finals MVP shared that he saw himself in another undersized guard, J.J. Barea, when he was handed a reserve point guard role.

"My mindset was, I'm filling JJ Barea's role. He came off the bench for Dallas. He did all these great things for Dallas.," he said.

"That's where I see myself. I'm gonna work to be better, but that's where I see myself. That's where I feel like I can help this team."

He excelled in that role. By his fourth year in Dallas, he had nearly doubled his production, going from 9.3 points per game during his rookie season to 16.3 in 2022.

Brunson believes his dedication to fulfilling the responsibilities of a role player gave him more opportunities to showcase his talent.

"The more you show in your role, the longer your leash gets, the more you're able to do. People just want to say, 'Hey, I can do this, I can do that.' Well, do what's asked of you first. Perfect it. Master it," he said.

"And all of a sudden you'll be surprised of what they'll allow you to do. And you'll be surprised by yourself, like, 'oh damn, I can do this.'"

After that, he signed with the Knicks. He is now a bona fide star.

He averaged 24 points per game in his first season in the Big Apple and 28.7 points per game the following season. He has been an All-Star in each of the last three seasons.

He is no longer a role player. Now, it is the role players who base their roles around him.

title: ‘Energy Level is High’ – 76ers Core Hold Workout Together and Jaylen Brown Can’t Contain His Excitement About His Group
description: Philadelphia 76ers fans have every reason to be excited about the upcoming season. They landed LeBron James and Jaylen Brown this summer. Chemistry is their next challenge, but it looks like it will not be much of a problem. NBA training camp will officially begin on September 29, but several teams have already taken steps [...]
fullText:
Philadelphia 76ers fans have every reason to be excited about the upcoming season. They landed LeBron James and Jaylen Brown this summer.

Chemistry is their next challenge, but it looks like it will not be much of a problem.

NBA training camp will officially begin on September 29, but several teams have already taken steps to build chemistry through workouts on their own time. The Sixers' core players are among them.

Brown said he has been working out with his new teammates, and he has a simple way of letting their supporters know that they are going to be good.

"We've been working, building chemistry with the guys. Maxey is a dog. LeBron is the goat, you don't even need to say what LeBron is. He look good, healthy," he said.

"This was one of our first workouts, but we worked out a few times. You can feel the energy level is high, the talent is high."

Brown and James join a team that surprised last season. The Sixers ended the regular season as the No. 2 seed and survived the play-in tournament to face JB's former team, the Boston Celtics. They went down 1-3 but still managed to beat them in seven games, powered by Joel Embiid's huge playoff performances and All-Star Tyrese Maxey.

Brown has been outspoken about the upcoming season following his shocking trade to the Sixers. He has released most of his statements through his Twitch streaming account.

In his latest episode, he expressed how mentally ready he is to play for the Sixers and how willing he is to make sacrifices to help them win a championship.

"Whatever the team needs, I'll be listening and waiting, but my mentality is to kill, you know what I mean? I feel like I want blood this year. I feel like that's the mentality: I want blood," he said.

Brown, James, Embiid, and Maxey are all expected to be part of the Sixers' starting five. They will be joined by VJ Edgecombe.

As for the bench, general manager Mike Gansey has added Anfernee Simons, Caleb Love, and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope. The team also has Dean Wade, Jabari Walker, and Justin Edwards.

ESPN's championship odds have the 76ers as the best team in the Eastern Conference, tied with the defending champion New York Knicks.

title: West Ham 4-2 Wolves - fans' verdict
description: We asked for your thoughts after Tuesday's Championship match between West Ham United and Wolverhampton Wanderers.
fullText:
We asked for your thoughts after Tuesday's Championship match between West Ham United and Wolverhampton Wanderers.

Here are some of your comments:

Woody: The game was a lottery as both defences were poor, but we managed to score more. We need to massively improve in defence if we're going to get promoted.

Dave: At last a better team effort, moving the ball quicker, but the new players we need didn't arrive.

At times the back four were wanting and the real big problem is that we don't have enough cover - what happened to finding full-back cover?

All we can do now is hope this team can continue with winning, but I am really concerned.

Sue: Much-improved display. The players need to gel and then will be a good competitive team. Still starting slow. That needs addressing.

Tristan: Didn't offer much at the back and were not clinical going forward at all. Played our hardest game of the season at a good time, and didn't make the most of it.

Steve: Overall I don't think we were that bad, certainly not 4-2 bad. We lost to yet another worldie, a daft, unnecessary penalty and a deflection, plus we hit the bar twice. It's a long season and it's going to be a rollercoaster - buckle up and stay positive.

Peter: Wolves will not be in the promotion stakes unless they tighten up their defence, which was cruelly exposed by the Hammers after looking suspect in the opening games. The retention of a focused Krejci and his return to the starting line-up could certainly help in that respect.

title: New York Giants' Darius Slayton addresses ongoing trade rumors
description: New York Giants wide receiver Darius Slayton shrugs off ongoing trade rumors and talks Odell Beckham Jr.
fullText:
Wide receiver Darius Slayton, the New York Giants' longest-tenured player, isn't about to let the recent trade rumors bother him. He's been the subject of that kind of talk before and has gotten used to it.

"It's not the first time, probably won't be the last time. But I really don't pay it too much of mind, honestly. I just take it day by day," he told reporters on Tuesday.

Slayton, 29, is entering the middle season of a three-year, $36 million deal with a $15.9 million salary cap hit for 2026. Those figures worked against the Giants in any trade talks. But they are working in Slayton's favor now. The Giants were rumored to be willing to move the former 2019 fifth-round pick out of Auburn this summer, but, as stated, his salary likely deterred any suitors.

The Giants had a glut of wideouts in camp and, even though Slayton was returning from sports hernia surgery this offseason, he was going to be included in the team's plans unless he could be moved in a trade. He made the Giants' 53-man roster this past weekend.

"I thought he played well. Had a heck of a camp," head coach John Harbaugh said. "He's a great guy, great player, hard worker, and did a heck of a job like he's always done here."

Slayton is just one of five wide receivers the Giants are carrying on their active roster, along with Malik Nabers, Malachi Fields, Darnell Mooney, and Odell Beckham Jr.

The 33-year-old Beckham's presence means Slayton is no longer the elder statesman in the Giants' wide receiver room.

Slayton came to the Giants the season after Beckham left via a trade with Cleveland. He is looking forward to playing with the former Pro Bowler and fan favorite.

"I think it's a beautiful thing for him to come back here,' said Slayton. "Obviously, the fans love him. If you're a football fan, you probably love him because he was such an iconic player. It's definitely awesome to see him get his chance to come back."

This article originally appeared on Giants Wire: New York Giants' Darius Slayton addresses ongoing trade rumors

title: Woltemade move underlines summer of change at Newcastle
description: It was ultimately a tale of two very different forwards on deadline day as Nick Woltemade left Newcastle United to join Juventus on loan and the club announced the arrival of Matias Fernandez-Pardo
fullText:
It was rather telling that Matias Fernandez-Pardo was Newcastle United's final signing of a rollercoaster summer.

This was a pursuit which was anything but straightforward.

The Belgian had been Newcastle's top target before the window opened, but it was only in the final stages of the summer that the club were able to complete a complex deal following delicate negotiations with Lille.

It was ultimately a tale of two very different forwards on deadline day.

On the same afternoon Newcastle announced the rapid Fernandez-Pardo's arrival, towering club-record signing Nick Woltemade finalised his loan move to Juventus.

Woltemade only joined Newcastle last summer, but this has been a window of change on Tyneside.

Head coach Eddie Howe stepped down in July and was replaced by Matthias Jaissle just a few weeks before the start of the new campaign.

Captain Bruno Guimaraes was among a handful of key players to leave while eight new signings arrived as Newcastle's records for spending and sales in a single window were both smashed.

This was the summer which altered the face of the club.

A shake-up had been signposted as far back as the spring.

It was in early April when Newcastle announced that defender Kieran Trippier would be leaving at the end of his contract.

The 34-year-old was approaching the twilight of his career, but his departure was still keenly felt as an influential figure behind the scenes.

"It was emotional for me, of course, because I loved the club so much and Newcastle gave me so much in return," the former England international said several months after moving on to Wolves.

"I'll always follow the club and want them to do well but, as a footballer, sometimes, you have to move on. With the utmost respect, I think it was the right time for both the club and myself.

"As I've always said, I wanted to leave in the right manner and show respect to my team-mates, the club and, most importantly, the supporters, who I have a great relationship with."

Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali's subsequent exits to Barcelona and Tottenham respectively did not necessarily come as a surprise, either, given they enabled Newcastle to comply and reinvest within the game's financial rules.

No-one internally had countenanced losing talisman Guimaraes, though.

However, having bailed Newcastle out so many times before, even the tireless midfielder dropped to the turf, untied his boots before the physio reached him and glared at the bench to come off during last season's final-day defeat at Fulham.

If ever an image summed up a bruising domestic campaign as Newcastle finished in 12th place - far below where the hierarchy had projected - and missed out on millions worth of European revenue.

The prospect of Guimaraes signing a new deal was unsurprisingly shot down by a figure involved in his subsequent £75m move to Arsenal a few weeks later.

After losing Alexander Isak to Liverpool against their wishes last summer, Newcastle ended up selling a fourth key player in less than a year.

They also missed out on top targets Victor Munoz and Johan Manzambi, who opted to move to Liverpool and Aston Villa respectively.

Yet those inside the club repeatedly stressed that the window could only be judged once it shut.

"Just because one element doesn't go the way you want doesn't mean you abandon the plan," a senior source said.

"We stayed on target, stayed focused, stayed calm and moved on. We didn't do a whole lot of mourning or crying when we had a setback.

The final fortnight of the summer ultimately proved critical as defender Amar Dedic, midfielder Nico Gonzalez and forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo all joined the club.

Season ticket holder Adam Widdrington believes the trio's arrivals and Newcastle's performances in the 2-2 draw against Liverpool and the 2-0 win at Tottenham Hotspur changed the narrative.

"Plenty of pundits and other fans had Newcastle earmarked for relegation," he said.

"They said, 'Who's the manager? Never heard of him. Who are these young players? You have lost a load of players'.

"I still wouldn't class it as a great transfer window, but I think it's a good one, especially given the context of where it looked like Newcastle were heading in that Bruno dip.

"At that point, it didn't feel like there was so much to inspire the fans, but the last three signings shifted opinion a lot."

Fernandez-Pardo certainly feels more of a stylistic fit for a side who made the most sprints in the opening weekend (138) of the Premier League season.

Jaissle has already cited the forward's "explosiveness" which, for all his endeavour, was not part of Woltemade's game, even during an impressive start to his Newcastle career a year ago.

Fernandez-Pardo will have to quickly adapt and there will inevitably be ups and downs as the campaign progresses for the 21-year-old and a young side.

"We always have hope and belief," Jaissle said before a ball had even been kicked this season. "No one can take that away from us."

Newcastle sign Fernandez-Pardo from Lille for £51m

Juventus sign Woltemade and Sarr on loan

title: Star Wars Zero Company review – joyfully absurd heroics with a tight-knit team of misfits
description:
PlayStation 5, Xbox Series S/X, PC; Bit Reactor
Split priorities between scripted and emergent story moments hamper an otherwise brilliant Star Wars-themed successor to XCOM
Even if you’re unfamiliar with the term “emergent storytelling”, you’ve likely experienced some of the unscripted tales that can bubble up out of a game’s systems. Perhaps you’ve led a scheming dynasty in Crusader Kings, or watched a favourite hero succumb to madness in Darkest Dungeon. Maybe you’ve surrendered yourself to the infinite yarn-spinner that is Dwarf Fortress – or read about it from the mid-00s forums where users helped popularise the term “Let’s Play” by chronicling their games in descriptive posts. Or perhaps you’ve played Firaxis’ XCOM, the alien invasion tactics hit that several key members of Zero Company studio Bit Reactor had a hand in.
Zero Company hinges on a concept as simple as it is perfect: take the complementary class abilities, tough dice rolls, and permanent character deaths of XCOM, and house them in a sci-fi setting known for spaghetti western blaster duels, last stands and heroic sacrifices.

Or perhaps you’ve played Firaxis’ XCOM, the alien invasion tactics hit that several key members of Zero Company studio Bit Reactor had a hand in.

Zero Company hinges on a concept as simple as it is perfect: take the complementary class abilities, tough dice rolls, and permanent character deaths of XCOM, and house them in a sci-fi setting known for spaghetti western blaster duels, last stands and heroic sacrifices. As creative director Greg Foertsch puts it, “Star Wars is about loss.” Which losses you end up mourning in Zero Company depends on you.

In theory, anyway. The game echoes Rogue One in its titular company of doomed misfits, but despite selling permadeath as a looming threat in the scripted tutorial, things rarely get dicey enough to put your squad in real danger. Even on its toughest difficulty, Zero Company feels reluctant to let a stray thermal detonator cut your companions’ stories short, blunting much of its potential for unscripted drama.

But in lieu of heroic sacrifices, Zcom (as I like to call it) is exceptional at telling a different kind of emergent story. Ones about iron-clad camaraderie and uneasy alliances. About the time your Mandalorian medic jetted in to heal your Jedi right on time, or the begrudging “nice shot” your clone trooper paid a former enemy sniper. The script feels designed to sell your mercenaries as an inseparable, dysfunctional family. Unironically, this one really is about the friends you make along the way.

Each fight is a reminder that Zero Company have each other’s backs. After an opening shot at enemy droids, you might have Kabb – a squat, bulbous alien scoundrel who speaks entirely in cutesy anastrophes – rush over and punch a hulking robot straight down a ravine. “What’s for supper? Cutty-upper!”, he declares for the third time in 15 minutes, met by some variations of “nicely done” from a random squadmate. Kabb’s still in bad shape from last turn, so you have your Astromech launch over healing stim. Kabb grabs it mid-air, slams it into his bicep, thanks the droid, and a notification tells you their bond has gotten stronger. That’ll mean a nice stat bump for them both later.

As all this happens, the battlefield buzzes with noise and motion. Idle combatants trade harmless potshots, ducking behind cover. Blaster holes sizzle through steel barriers. Battle Droids mock your missed shots, babbling “oh no!” like exploding lemmings when their comrades fall. There is so much personality in the different ways characters move. Gangers scramble down ladders. Astromechs bump into crates, then jump-jet over. Jedi leap and flip, and droids curl and spin like chrome woodlice. Through it all, veteran Star Wars composer Gordy Haab underscores every peril and triumph, paying pitch-perfect tribute to the textures of John Williams’ original score.

Between missions, you’ll return to the Den: a streamlined but engaging take on the customisation and upgrades of XCOM’s command centre, with the hangout space of Mass Effect’s Normandy. Via a galaxy map, you’ll spend intel, collect rewards, and make tough choices about which upgrades to deny your foes. It’s also here you’ll learn about your crew’s pasts. If you’ve got the time, you can even join them on personal quests.

I haven’t mentioned Zero Company’s overarching plot so far, mainly because there’s little worth mentioning. Its central threat, the Infinite Coil, are a tiresomely exoticised, first-draft cult with ill-defined goals, evidently concocted because the combat needed an enemy faction with some flavour of space magic for variety’s sake. The enemy’s reliance on healing and damage negation – a clumsy workaround for AI that can’t keep up with your team’s escalating stats and skills – results in some laborious late-game encounters.

These are by far the weakest parts of an otherwise brilliant debut from Bit Reactor, however. And even when the plot falters, touching character moments join digestible, deeply human explorations of this era of Star Wars’ byzantine factional politics. XCOM’s success has influenced countless turn-based tactics games. Few have made squeezing joyfully absurd heroics out of a handful of action points feel this good. Fewer have made me grin so hard at a final lucky shot during a last-second evacuation. That’s my squad down there, after all.

Star Wars: Zero Company is out now: £39.99

title: ‘We have had enough’: thousands of University of Sydney staff walk off the job over AI and job security
description: Hundreds of university staff were stationed at picket lines, calling for stronger protections around the use of...
fullText:
Hundreds of university staff were stationed at picket lines, calling for stronger protections around the use of AI

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The same week union members at the University of Sydney agreed to a 24-hour strike, staff received the results of an internal survey.

In the faculty of arts and social sciences, 0% agreed with the statement: “I trust the University of Sydney to act in the best interests of staff, students and the broader community.”

It was the issue of trust, alongside longstanding concerns over staff protections from artificial intelligence, workload fairness and job security, that saw about 2,000 members to walk off the job on Wednesday.

From 7am, about 500 people were stationed at picket lines at each of the inner Sydney campus’s entrances, armed with flags, banners and megaphones.

The University of Sydney advised students “almost all” scheduled classes would move online as a result of the strike, while others were rescheduled or cancelled.

Peter Chen, the branch president of the National Tertiary Education Union (NTEU) at the University of Sydney, said management had rebuffed the union “at every opportunity” to enforce appropriate protections around the use of AI.

“Higher education is the canary in the coalmine,” he said. “Where we go on AI … will travel through the rest of the economy.”

The New South Wales division secretary of the NTEU, Vince Caughley, said the University of Sydney’s own green paper advised AI was the most “fundamental transformation” education had seen, pointing to AI chatbots that were already being used to help teach online-only classes at other universities.

“We are asking for best practice, we are asking for due diligence,” he said. “Not their own commercialisation aims and certainly not the interest of venture capital.”

The union was confident it would reach an agreement with management within the year but had concerns over the lack of senior leadership at the table, including the provost, Prof Annamarie Jagose. The last bargaining process represented the longest running industrial action at an Australian university, and the prospect of future strikes remained active.

A spokesperson for the University of Sydney said it was “continuing to engage” with the union and maintained industrial action was “premature”.

“We agree using AI ethically requires a human-centred approach, and our … principles and guardrails that govern use have been developed in consultation with our community,” they said.

“We support many of the objectives of the unions’ claims, but believe it’s more appropriate to implement many of these through relevant policies, instead of in the Enterprise Agreement.”

There are broader concerns, some interlinked and widespread in the sector. Growing class sizes and reduced student satisfaction. A new proposal for teaching-only roles with no research component or scope for future growth.

Prof Laura Shepherd in the school of social and political sciences is part of the bargaining team and said students often sacrificed a “huge amount” to come to the university, including spending $50,000 on degrees.

“They come here … for quality and access to research leaders,” she said. “I think we should be very ashamed if we allow anything in the enterprise agreement that threatens that.”

The University of Sydney’s NTEU branch is the largest in Australia, and the university has long been a hotbed for activism. As management approaches its fifth month of bargaining, it is also grappling with continued opposition to its response to Gaza and restrictions on protest.

New restrictions were brought in as a result of the university’s pro-Palestine encampment in 2024, which received intense scrutiny during this year’s royal commission. On Wednesday, keffiyehs and pro-Palestine banners stood out among purple NTEU flags and signage.

The Student Representative Council was also striking in solidarity with staff and picketing online classes. Its education officer, Dana Kafina, said the university’s “draconian” protest restrictions were a motivation.

“In the wake of … suppressions of free speech and activism, and some of the lowest rates of student and graduate satisfaction in the country, we have had enough,” she said.

Despite the presence of campus security and police, the picket lines had a jovial atmosphere. Some blasted music on speakers, others banged drums and chanted with abandon.

Kurt Iveson, a professor of geography, was among them, running a quiz on his megaphone as, behind him, students sold baked goods to raise funds for lost income of strikers.

Iveson has been with the university for 20 years, and wants “meaningful protections” that do not outlaw AI but ensure “the tech is serving our purpose, rather than us serving the tech”.

“All of us on the picket line today are here because we care so much about the education and research we do,” he said.

title: SERV – The SErial RISC-V CPU Topics
description: SERV - The SErial RISC-V CPU. Contribute to olofk/serv development by creating an account on GitHub.
fullText:
SERV is an award-winning bit-serial RISC-V core

In fact, the award-winning SERV is the world's smallest RISC-V CPU. It's the perfect companion whenever you need a bit of computation and silicon real estate is at a premium.

How small is it then? Synthesizing the latest version of SERV in its most minimal form, yields the following results for some popular FPGA architectures and a typical CMOS process.

If you want to know more about SERV, what a bit-serial CPU is and what it's good for, I recommend starting out by watching the fantastic short SERV movies

All SERV videos and more can also be found here.

Apart from being the world's smallest RISC-V CPU, SERV also aims at being the best documented RISC-V CPU. For this there is an official SERV user manual with block diagrams that are correct to the gate-level, cycle-accurate timing diagrams and an in-depth description of how things work.

SERV is open source released under the ISC license. If you need a commercial license with patent grants, professional paid support or added features, please contact olof@award-winning.me

SERV can be easily integrated into any design, but if you are looking at just quickly trying it out, here is a list of some systems that are already using SERV:

Servant is the reference platform for SERV. It is a very basic SoC that contains just enough to run Zephyr RTOS. Servant is intended for FPGAs and has been ported to around 20 different FPGA boards. It is also used to run the RISC-V regression test suite.

CoreScore is an award-giving benchmark for FPGAs and their synthesis/P&R tools. It tests how many SERV cores that can be put into a particular FPGA.

Observer is a configurable and software-programmable sensor aggregation platform for heterogeneous sensors.

Subservient is a small technology-independent SERV-based SoC intended for ASIC implementations together with a single-port SRAM.

Litex is a Python-based framework for creating FPGA SoCs. SERV is one of the 30+ supported cores. A Litex-generated SoC has been used to run DooM on SERV.

⭕ Create a directory to keep all the different parts of the project together.

Create and export an environment variable, WORKSPACE, for easy reference to that directory:

Each of the following commands should be run from the workspace directory:

Add the FuseSoC standard library

The FuseSoC standard library already contain a version of SERV, but if we want to make changes to SERV, run the bundled example or use the Zephyr support, it is better to add SERV as a separate library into the workspace

📘 The SERV repo will now be available in $WORKSPACE/fusesoc_libraries/serv. We will refer to that directory as $SERV.

Create and export its environment variable

Install the latest version of Verilator

(Optional) To support RISC-V M extension, Multiplication and Division unit (MDU) can be included in SERV as a separate library.

MDU will be available in $WORKSPACE/fusesoc_libraries/mdu

📗 We are now ready to do our first exercises with SERV. If everything above is done correctly, we can use Verilator as a linter to check the SERV source code.

If everything worked, the output should look like

After performing all the steps that are mentioned above, the directory structure from the $WORKSPACE should look like this:

Build and run the single threaded zephyr hello world example with verilator (should be stopped with Ctrl-C):

..or... the multithreaded version

Both should yield an output ending with

For a more advanced example, we can also run the Dining philosophers demo

...or... the synchronization example

...or... the blinky example (note that the uart_baudrate should not be defined for the blinky test)

If the toolchain is installed, other applications can be tested by compiling the assembly program and converting to bin and then hex with makehex.py found in $SERV/sw.

💡RISC-V Compressed Extension can be enabled by passing --compressed=1 parameter.

SERV is verified using RISC-V compliance tests for the base ISA (RV32I) and the implemented extensions (M, C, Zicsr). The instructions on running Compliance tests using RISCOF framework are given in verif directory.

The above targets are run on the servant SoC, but there are some targets defined for the CPU itself. Verilator can be run in lint mode to check for design problems by running

It's also possible to just synthesise for different targets to check resource usage and such. To do that for the iCE40 devices, run

...or to synthesize with vivado for Xilinx targets, run

This will synthesize for the default Vivado part. To synthesise for a specific device, run e.g.

SERV, or rather the Servant SoC, can run the Zephyr RTOS. The Servant-specific drivers and BSP is located in the zephyr subdirectory of the SERV repository. In order to use Zephyr on Servant, a project directory structure must be set up that allows Zephyr to load the Servant-specific files as a module.

First, the Zephyr SDK and the "west" build tool must be installed. The Zephyr getting started guide describes these steps in more detail.

Assuming that SERV was installed into $WORKSPACE/fusesoc_libraries/serv as per the prerequisites, run the following command to make the workspace also work as a Zephyr workspace.

Specify the SERV repository as the manifest repository, meaning it will be the main entry point when Zephyr is looking for modules.

Get the right versions of all Zephyr submodules

It should now be possible to build Zephyr applications for the Servant SoC within the workspace. This can be tested e.g. by building the Zephyr Hello world samples application

After a successful build, Zephyr will create an elf and a bin file of the application in build/zephyr/zephyr.{elf,bin}. The bin file can be converted to a verilog hex file, which in turn can be preloaded to FPGA on-chip memories and run on a target board, or loaded into simulated RAM model when running simulations.

To convert the newly built hello world example into a Verilog hex file, run

4096 is the number of 32-bit words to write and must be at least the size of the application binary. hello.hex is the resulting hex file. Running a simulation can now be done as described in Running pre-built test software, e.g.

Or to create an FPGA image with the application preloaded to on-chip RAM, e.g. for a Nexys A7 board, run

Don't feed serv any illegal instructions after midnight. Many logic expressions are hand-optimized using the old-fashioned method with Karnaugh maps on paper, and shamelessly take advantage of the fact that some opcodes aren't supposed to appear. As serv was written with 4-input LUT FPGAs as target, and opcodes are 5 bits, this can save quite a bit of resources in the decoder.

The bus interface is kind of Wishbone, but with most signals removed. There's an important difference though. Don't send acks on the instruction or data buses unless serv explicitly asks for something by raising its cyc signal. Otherwise serv becomes very confused.

Don't go changing the clock frequency on a whim when running Zephyr. Or well, it's ok I guess, but since the UART is bitbanged, this will change the baud rate as well. As of writing, the UART is running at 115200 baud rate when the CPU is 32 MHz. There are two NOPs in the driver to slow it down a bit, so if those are removed I think it could achieve baud rate 115200 on a 24MHz clock.. in case someone wants to try
